speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, May 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet (for Mr. Gray) that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on Bill C-24, which is an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof. For my part I would like to discuss the legislation within the broader framework of government intervention. Rather than restricting this, the Bill gives the Government increased regulatory power and is therefore typical of the excessive desire on the part of the Government to control, to keep secret and to insulate, from both parliamentary scrutiny and public scrutiny, Acts of Parliament.
My strongest belief, as a former businessman and now as an elected representative, is that if private enterprise can do the job as well or better than government, then the state should not interfere. Where government intervention is necessary, it must be conducted in a spirit of co-operation and accommodation, not in competition with the private sector. I am sure the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development (Mr. Johnston) would share this opinion if given the opportunity to express himself freely and free of Cabinet.
If in fact private enterprise is to be successful, the Government must immediately stop creating impediments to growth and allow the small-businessman the chance to expand and stimulate employment opportunities within his sector. Economic recovery is dependent upon developing the creative capacity of the private sector. Yet the Government continues to interfere in the economy, either directly or indirectly, through mechanisms such as Crown corporations. This constant interference in the marketplace has stifled private initiative and has suppressed investment capital which is so badly needed for job creation. If we are truly interested in creating
jobs we need working capital. We have to encourage investment in the private sector, not discourage it. Confirmation of this is provided by the alarming trend developing which is effectively reversing the role of government accountability.
Today the attitude which is prevalent at many levels of the federal bureaucracy is that somehow the taxpayer is accountable to government, not the government accountable to the taxpayer. This is not at all surprising, considering the overwhelming growth of government which has taken place over the past 15 years.
The enormous size of government all but eliminates personal accountability for the economical, efficient and effective management of public funds. During the years of bureaucratic expansion, it appears that the public purse was deemed to be bottomless. All of this uncontrolled growth is designed for the purpose of allowing government increasingly to interfere in the process of free enterprise.
These concerns were expressed very clearly and were shared by the former U.S. Treasury Secretary, William Simon. He said:
People must be taught to start calling for a rollback of the bureaucracy, where nothing will be lost but strangling regulation and where gains will always take the form of liberty, productivity and jobs.
In Canada today we are witnessing the growth of a disease of government which, if it is allowed to proceed unchecked, will reap untold destruction. Yet Government Members express shock when we criticize a Bill which, far from improving the situation, will only make matters worse by extending the discretionary powers of government and Crown corporations. There is, unfortunately, no shortage of evidence to support the claim that is being made on behalf of the Opposition. To quote page 13 of the Auditor General's report, he noted:
It may be helpful in visualizing the scale of the problem to think of the whole group as an enormous iceberg floating lazily in the foggy Atlantic; silent, majestic, awesome. The public tends to see only the upper portions,... the giants like CNR, Petro-Can, CBC,... The great bulk of the iceberg below the surface is less spectacular, less likely to attract public interest, less likely to receive the attention of Parliament, yet costly to the taxpayers.
A list of "wild risks" and "unknown losers" include "the boat that wouldn't float". Between January, 1973 and June, 1979, the Government spent $1.4 million on a fisheries training vessel which was supposed to cost only $308,000 to purchase and refit. The Government of Columbia refused to accept the vessel due to its instability and unsuitability, according to the Auditor General's report of 1979.
Let us take a look at Consolidated Computer Inc. It was a government experiment to take an equity position in this

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
computer company, which it was subsidizing, and it ultimately cost the Canadian taxpayer $124 million. The company was finally dumped. That is proof evident of the inability of the Government to compete with the private sector. Let us look at Maislin Transport Ltd. In spite of being told not to by officials in the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the federal Government guaranteed a $33.4 million loan to Maislin in July of 1982. A year later the company declared bankruptcy.
In February, 1981 the federal Government purchased Petrofina for approximately $1.46 billion, or $120 per share. At the time of the purchase the shares were trading for $90 and were estimated by various brokerage houses to have a true value of about $80. In other words, the federal Government paid between $365 million and $486 million more than was necessary in order to acquire a chain of gasoline stations in eastern Canada.
The carrying costs of the money invested by the Government to date in Petro-Canada totals over $700 million. It is important to remember that Petro-Canada was originally intended to give Canada a window on the oil industry. For the amount of taxpayers' dollars spent to date, I certainly hope we have a good view. However, I am not so sure the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development would agree. For instance, on April 8, 1984, he had this to say about the "people's" company:
I don't see any need for Petro-Canada in the service station business. I don't see that the Government needs to retail gas any more than it needs to retail chocolates-
If someone came with a good offer for the Petro-Canada service stations, I would be the first to recommend that they be sold provided we are satisfied that the same service is going to be given to the public.
It is strange yet somewhat refreshing to observe a Liberal Cabinet Minister voice his concerns for free enterprise. I wonder where his recently established sense of conviction was when his accomplices and their bureaucratic experts fashioned the National Energy Program.
Government has to start slowing down on its involvement in the private sector. It is most important that when we look at Crown corporations, we assess them from the standpoint of their necessity, not from the standpoint of the necessity of government to get involved in the marketplace. I would hope that where the private sector is serving the Canadian people well, the Government would stay out of the marketplace and leave it up to that sector. That is the sector which can best manage our economy.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I assure you that I will speak sufficiently slowly that even those people who do not understand Ukrainian will understand what I am saying.
I appreciate the opportunity to participate in this debate today and to deal with this legislative initiative which has been taken by the Government with respect to Crown corporations in our country. People who are following the debate will understand that there has been of recent months and years a very substantial concern expressed by many Canadians about the whole question of accountability of Crown corporations. I know that people in my own constituency have asked me how it can be that corporations such as Canadair and de Havilland, by way of example-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
PWA is a money maker. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) will know that when the Conservatives get their hands on these things, proper management and accountability prevails. However, I will save that for another debate, Mr. Speaker. I simply wanted to deal at this point in time with the whole question of accountability in terms of the intentions of the Government in this Bill.
Then, to deal with something which has not yet really been covered in this debate, there is the problem, as I see it, of two sets of standards; one for Crown corporations and one for the average Canadian. I refer to the principle of Crown immunity. That simply means that whenever an agency or an official of an agency of government is involved in activities ostensibly dealing with the performance of the duties of government, they are protected from prosecution, criminal or otherwise. For example, if I were to try and set up a cartel, within Canada or internationally, I could expect to be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law by officials of the Crown. By the same token, if I were involved in misleading or false advertising, the people of Canada would say that it is against the law and that person or company should be prosecuted.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, Canadian Crown corporations occupy a privileged place with respect to the laws of this land. Crown corporations, agencies and Cabinet Ministers involved in direct competition with the private sector do not have to obey the law. They have the defence of Crown immunity. I think most Canadians would ask how this can possibly be. They think we live in a country with a government under the rule of law, which means not only the governed have to obey the law but governments also have to obey the law. I am sure the people do not realize that if government agencies and Crown corporations involved in commercial activities mislead the public by false advertising or involve themselves in cartels, they cannot be prosecuted. But the law says that is the case. Section 16 of the Interpretation Act deals with Her Majesty as follows:
No enactment is binding on Her Majesty or affects Her Majesty or Her Majesty's rights or prerogatives in any manner, except only as therein mentioned or referred to.
That means that the agents of Her Majesty, the Government of Canada, are not affected by the criminal law in this country unless there is a specific inclusion in the legislation to make them liable. Crown corporations continue to enjoy spe-
May 7, 1984

cial status and they carry on business in the public domain, but they are not subject to the laws of the land. Since Crown corporations have immunity, they can break the law with impunity. There is no way to achieve redress through the courts of our land. We have one law for the Government, and another for you and me, Mr. Speaker, the governed of this country.
We all know the sordid history of the uranium cartel which took place under this Government. Involved were the present Minister of State for Social Development, Senator Austin in the other place, the Deputy Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in charge of Uranium Canada and Eldorado Nuclear Limited, and others. These people and the Cabinet Ministers involved actually travelled around the world to set up a cartel with respect to the world price of uranium. This cartel was established. As a result, literally hundreds of thousands of Canadians paid unreasonable and unrealistic prices for uranium for the generation of power. The people in the Province of Ontario paid very large amounts due to this illegal activity. The Government of Canada initiated this activity and was the main force involved in the formation of the cartel.
Mir. Orlikow: Did the Ontario Government know about it?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Government of Ontario was completely oblivious, Mr. Speaker, to this whole situation. I always have to inform Members of the NDP about the facts of life. During my political life I have been trying to be helpful to that Party. They do not take my advice and look where they are in the polls. It is just awful. I do not know what I can do to salvage this Party, but I am working as hard as I can in the best interests of the people of Canada and the NDP to make sure that justice prevails.
In December of 1983 the Supreme Court of Canada handed down a decision which, in effect, said that Eldorado Nuclear and Uranium Canada could not be charged for their part in this cartel. They have been exempted. However, all the private concerns which were forced, by virtue of government directives, either to participate in this activity or be out of the picture as far as uranium sales are concerned find their positions in jeopardy. These private companies are taking the full brunt of the prosecution.
The Government is relying on this defence to protect itself and its political friends. Even under the freedom of information legislation the Government will not release documents pertaining to the formation of this cartel. That indicates the power the Government has. In our country we pride ourselves on the principle that the Government operates under the rules of law. That is why it is absolutely essential that we study this legislation to ensure that those who are involved in government are not exempted by their own legislation from any accountability to the courts or the Parliament of this land.
I could give you other examples with respect to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, Mr. Speaker. A matter was raised with respect to what many people in Canada
Financial Administration Act
considered to be misleading advertising. I see I have only a couple of minutes remaining, but I have a letter dated September 10, 1980 from Consumer and Corporate Affairs to Murray Coolican of the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee in Ottawa. In this letter K. G. Decker, Director of the Marketing Practices Branch, said:
In addition, there have been some cases in law which appear to have established that agents of the Crown, which would include most government departments, cannot be prosecuted.
I raised in the House of Commons the matter of the Royal Canadian Mint, another Crown corporation, advertising silver dollars which in fact were 50 per cent alloy and 50 per cent silver. There was nothing in the advertising which told the Canadian consumer that. Simpsons Limited was prosecuted for advertising jewellery which was not all it was cracked up to be. They were fined $1 million. Of course, there has been no prosecution of the Royal Canadian Mint for misleading advertising.
I have really only started, Mr. Speaker, but I will conclude this part of my remarks on this issue. I know there has been some discussion about changing the competition laws of the country. In this legislation we need a provision to ensure that Crown corporations operate under the same rules as every other company or citizen of the country.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great respect that I enter this debate to follow those Hon. Members in our caucus who have had many years of parliamentary experience and give a background of Crown corporations in order to let Canadians fully understand the difficulties of Crown corporation operations.
There is a story which I believe helps to explain the problems caused by Crown corporations in Canada and other countries assuming an increasing role in the economic and regulatory activities of a country. It is a story by Barbara Tuchman entitled "The March of Folly". The story is about King Philip of Spain who reigned during the seventeenth century. It is said that he died of a fever which was contracted by sitting too long beside a stove. The problem was that he was unable to find the public servant to turn down the temperature of the stove. This story reflects the difficulty that takes place when people who are not fully accountable or sensitive to what should happen carry out an operation for which the Government is responsible.
While King Philip met his end in an extraordinary way, I do not know whether it will be so obvious when we are consumed by the inability to gain control of the activities being undertaken on our behalf by public servants and others in Crown corporations. However, it is a clear demonstration of the dangers and difficulties that exist in Crown corporations. When one considers the ever-increasing involvement of government in the lives of Canadians, the point raised in this story about accountability and communication becomes more important.

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
The level of government activity in our daily lives has reached a tremendous proportion, up to 47 per cent of our Gross National Product. This demonstrates the need for more effective management and ability to control and direct this level of activity on our own behalf.
I would also question why we are dealing with a Bill such as Bill C-24 at this time. What is so important about its need today as compared to the last 15 years during which time these difficulties with Crown corporations have been identified by past Auditor Generals and numerous politicians from both sides of the House? These difficulties have been pointed out most recently by one of the Liberal leadership candidates who indicated with respect to Petro-Canada that he would like to make changes and sell some of the gas stations.
While these difficulties have been outlined for some time now, we are suddenly faced with Bill C-24. I guess something is better than nothing and that this Bill has some relevance in that at least some action is finally being taken to come to grips with this problem. However, some of the most important authorities throughout the country have not had an adequate opportunity to study this Bill in detail, to consider its consequences or suggest amendments to address these problems which we have known about for some time.
The Hon. Member who spoke before me indicated several specific examples of the problems which could develop. Due to his full knowledge and understanding of particular areas, such as the uranium cartel and so on, I think he is adequately qualified to point out how this Bill should be modified so that it does not end up as legislation that will not achieve the goals which we set out.
Of course, one of the main goals is to achieve accountability and ensure that Crown corporations have an obligation to serve the public interest while at the same time Ministers and the Government accept the responsibility for their direction. I believe the present legislation will continue to allow Crown corporations to take the responsibility which should be that of the Government in terms of management, personnel and other factors. While political initiative may be behind the action of the corporation, this Bill does not provide for the political responsibility of that action. There could be cases where capable, competent public servants, who may be able to produce a satisfactory result if left to their own resources, may have been interfered with by the political process which in turn has not been accountable for those activities.
In the few minutes remaining, let me proceed to the question of immunity from prosecution according to other Acts. If Crown corporations are to be any value, they will have to be subject to the same laws of the land as other Crown corporations within our economic environment. An excellent example of this was Eldorado Nuclear. In that instance the Combines Investigation Act should have applied. If this Bill is passed in its present form, I suggest that the Cabinet will be the real winner. It will not be Canadians who deserve to have sufficient accountability and the political responsibility which they can judge at the time of a general election. However, this legislation provides the Cabinet with many opportunities to avoid
some of the responsibilities and escape some of the controlled mechanisms that should be consistently applied across the board, as was the intent of this very legislation.
In closing, let me comment on this massive government within government, as it has been described by one Auditor General, which exceeds even the current personnel of the Public Service. I think Canadians must come to grips with what is not necessarily a problem of government or Crown corporations but an effect of human nature. I believe it is human nature for all of us to try to achieve as much as possible with as little effort as possible, whether it is in a public activity, political or private enterprise. Therefore, unless there is accountability and an entire range of requirements for responsibility to carry out particular objectives, we will all lose a very great deal.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) who spoke earlier, I had the impression that he and perhaps some of his colleagues were so wedded to the free enterprise system that they are opposed to any and all Crown corporations. I want to remind him that Crown corporations are as Canadian as apple pie. Crown corporations have been created by federal and provincial governments that were Liberal, Conservative, NDP and even Social Credit. They were created by these governments when they came to the conclusion that the free enterprise system was not ready to take the risk. It could not see its way to making a profit in a field which was socially or economically necessary.
And so you have the Ontario Hydro which was created many years ago by a Conservative Government. You have the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta telephone systems. These are all Crown corporations. Manitoba's Crown corporation was created by a Conservative Government way back in 1907 led by Sir R. P. Roblin. You have the B.C. Hydro created as a public utility by a Social Credit Government. We ought to keep in mind that Crown corporations have been established because they were needed. That does not mean Crown corporations, like privately-owned corporations, need not be monitored, examined and watched to see they do the things which they were created to do. But to operate them as efficiently and as economically as possible, Mr. Speaker, the public needs as much information as possible. A government which creates Crown corporations, be it a federal or provincial government, needs the authority to see that its Crown corporations do the jobs they are supposed to.
There has been a lot of evidence of this, Mr. Speaker. I have given you de Havilland, Canadair and Atomic Energy of Canada, all of which got into trouble. Not only did they get into trouble but it was obvious they were not reporting to government as they should concerning their troubles and what could and should have been done about them. To the extent that this Bill improves the situation by giving government and, therefore, Parliament the authority and power to correct situations which are improper, we will support the Bill.
May 7, 1984

I want to spend a few minutes now discussing the problems of one Crown corporation which we believe should not be included under the terms of this Bill. I am speaking of the Canada Council. We think the inclusion of the Canada Council under the provisions of Bill C-24 is wrong. We feel the Government has made a serious error in this regard. We believe it is totally inappropriate for the Government to put an agency such as the Canada Council under the provisions of Bill C-24. We believe that the Canada Council Act as it now stands does everything which Bill C-24 would do, but it enables the Canada Council to maintain its independent position free from the influence of politically motivated decisions.
Over the past 25 years the Canada Council has established a reputation for quality of work, delivery of service, and support to the Canadian cultural community. This reputation was built on the principle that government in Canada should support the flourishing of culture and art in our country. But an independent body controlled by bona fide representatives of the arts and cultural community should make the difficult judgments about which artists and cultural endeavours should be funded by government.
Let me point out that the Canada Council was established in 1957 as a result of the recommendations of the Massey-Levesque Royal Commission on the Arts, Letters and Social Sciences in Canada. At that time the Commission stated in its report:
We should ... consider it a misfortune if this Canada Council became in any sense a department of government, but we realize that since this body will be spending public money it must be in an effective manner responsible to the Government and hence to parliament.
With the Canada Council we are not dealing with a massive corporation such as some I have mentioned, like de Havilland, Canadair or Atomic Energy of Canada. They are Crown corporations which spend hundreds of millions of dollars. We are dealing with a rather small and specialized organization which has always been clearly recognized as a promoter of culture, apart and independent from direct political influence. If Bill C-24 is passed into law without change and the Canada Council is included in the new Bill, it will therefore fall under the provisions of the Financial Administration Act.
It was a Liberal Prime Minister, Mr. St. Laurent, when introducing the Canada Council Act to Parliament, who stated that the Council should be independent because governments should, and I quote:
-support the cultural development of the nation but not control it.
Bill C-24 directly contradicts the opinion of the arts community and overturns the principle of an arm's length relationship established by the Massey Commission and the Liberal Government of the day. We ask ourselves why. We think it is for bureaucratic consistency, to satisfy those minds concerned with building better paper empires, more fundamentally perhaps to give senior departmental officials control of cultural development and to politicize the process of the distribution of cultural funds even more. We have seen that kind of politicization in almost every aspect of this Government's operations. We think that has been bad. We think to begin to apply that to
Financial Administration Act
the Canada Council and to the arts and cultural community would be a major mistake.
As it operates now, the Canada Council is fully audited by the Auditor General every year, unlike the Crown corporation giants which are more correctly the prime targets of this Bill, and so they should be, Mr. Speaker. The Canada Council fully discloses the names of the organizations and individuals that receive its grants as well as the names of its members and its jurors. These are published in the annual report. Along with this, representatives of the Canada Council appear before Commons committees and other official bodies. They make reports and are subject to questioning on a regular basis.
The requirements of the Financial Administration Act will impose greater administrative costs upon the Canada Council and effectively reduce the already limited funding that the Council must allocate to the arts and cultural community. Under the provisions of Bill C-24, the 21-member board of the Canada Council will have reduced powers and be more subject to the imperatives of departmental officials with the almost certain result that the actions and decisions of the Council will suffer. Specifically the quality of judgment and the decisions made in allocating funds for cultural and artistic endeavours will deteriorate. The needs and priorities of the arts will fall victim to the closer relationship the Council will be bound to have with the Department of Communications.
We believe the Canada Council has over the 27 years of its existence shown itself to be an innovative and active organization using a relatively effective peer judgment system to allocate scarce funding to the Canadian artistic and intellectual community. In doing so it has nurtured research and creation in the fields of social sciences, arts, drama and music and it has produced valuable cultural achievements.
The implications of Bill C-24 are, in the case of the Canada Council, completely inappropriate. This Bill will contribute nothing to making the Council more effective in accomplishing its objectives. The Bill must be amended in order that the Canada Council is excluded from its provisions, just as other specialized agencies of the Government have been excluded.

Mr. Speaker, the opportunity to speak on a Bill like this does not come too often. I am very pleased this Bill has now come to this Parliament, as it has to several other Parliaments through which we have sat. Bill C-24 deals with the organization and operation of Crown corporations to a great degree.
At first glance it would appear that this Bill will give the Government even more power. The Bill does not in any way clarify or specify how the Government intends to use this control of the various Crown corporations for the good of the general public, the taxpayer, or indeed of the corporations.
This Government has, of course, a long record of its treatment of Crown corporations, almost uniformly bad. I can easily agree with the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow). He pointed out that Crown corporations are supposed to be created to serve the good of the public, when there is a need for a public service that may be lost if the Crown

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
does not come to the rescue. That does not mean that the present Government understands its role in Crown corporations. One suspects that the real reason for many of the Crown corporations the Government has adopted lately is that it wishes the Crown to own as much as it can of the industry in this country. Among the reasons it places very high on the scale is the location of the Crown corporation, which Members of Parliament will be affected and what kind of berth it might provide for some of its former Members or some who will be leaving in the near future.
I would like to deal with the problem of the aircraft industry in Canada in particular. This brings us to Canadair and de Havilland. I and many of my colleagues sat in this Parliament in 1974 when this subject was a matter of active discussion. It is like a page from ten years ago to see the Hon. John Turner discussing what he would do. He was the leader in the movement for the Government to go to Crown corporations.
Despite his record of doubling the deficit, he now holds himself up as the champion of halving the deficit. The question of whether he is able to divide as easily as he was able to multiply is something the voters will have to answer, and maybe even John Turner.
When we debated this some ten years ago, the Government was clearly warned what kind of mess it was getting into if it got into the aircraft industry. My friend from York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) spoke on April 2, 1974. He pointed out that the Government and the NDP were of one mind, that they were lusting for power. At page 1095 of Hansard, the Hon. Member for York-Peel said:
I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in particular should note that these Members will buy anything sight unseen. When we attempted to have the estimate with respect to de Havilland reduced in committee. Government Members, joined by their allies in the NDP, said, "We don't care what the statement of de Havilland looks like. We don't care whether or not it is earning money. We want that estimate to go through".
The Hon. Member for York-Peel had come across information showing that while the Government was attempting to buy this corporation, it had sales valued at S35 million and was marginally profitable. At the same time the subsidiary of Hawker-Siddeley, England, Hawker-Siddeley of Canada, had sales of $200 million and profitability after taxation of $3 million. We bought the one with the smallest possible profitability and the lower sales. The Government was not interested in buying the one that was a going concern. That was typical of the attitude of the then Minister of Finance. He was totally supported by his chief rival at the meeting in Halifax yesterday. The then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, now Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), said some things which make for comic relief, knowing what we know now about his pet project, Canadair.
This hearkens back to the politics concerned. This company was located in the constituency of Dollard, the preserve of the then Minister of Supply and Services, the Hon. J. P. Goyer. He turned out to be an executive of Canadair when it became fully nationalized and needed some inexpert directors in which
this Government's Crown corporations seem to abound. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) was extolling this jump into the future that he had brought about. On March 8, 1977 he said in the House of Commons:
I might talk for a few seconds, with your permission, about the famous LearStar jet project. I was asked questions in the House this afternoon on that matter. This is becoming one of the greatest success stories in the history of industrial development in Canada. Within three months, we have already sold 71 aircraft at a cost of some $5 million each. The prototype is not even completed but a combination of factors, the fact that it is a long-range plane with a range of over 5,000 miles and a fuel consumption of approximately two thirds that of competitive aircraft, the fact that the demand is greater for that type of plane since many air services have been discontinued throughout the world and executives feel the need to buy planes for their business trips, and also that we now have the expertise in Canada to build that plane, for all these reasons it is a very exciting program.
We could do with a little less excitement and a little more business sense. He is the second choice for the leadership of the Party across the way.
One yearns for one of the few moments of truth that one has heard from Government Ministers in this regard. When the Hon. Jack Horner was Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, I asked whether it was still the policy of the Government to sell to private industry the combined air industry which the Government claimed was the reason for nationalizing both of these companies. To his credit, Mr. Horner said that they had run into a problem: when they were losing money, nobody wanted to buy the company, and when they were making money, they did not want to sell. That was possibly the last totally honest answer we have had on this subject in this Parliament.
If one looks at Schedule C-II showing which corporations are being put in this Bill, you find that the Canada Development Investment Corporation in 1982 had a deficit of $1.7 billion. This was largely brought about by Canadair having a deficit of $1.4 billion. Several times the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and Cabinet Ministers have been questioned about this. Their answer is: "Do you want to lose the expertise? Do you want to lose the jobs?" It is a sad tale if a company is not able to produce a viable product. However, there must be a limit as to how much you are willing to spend for jobs. Since Canadair has approximately 1,400 employees, it is very easy to figure out what the jobs cost when you have a deficit in one year of $1.4 billion: it comes to $1 million per job. That is a little more than any economy can bear, to be losing $1 million per job created.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but his time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, we are debating Bill C-24, the Financial Administration Act, a Bill with a magnitude we cannot predict in terms of its effect on the economic health of our country. It is discouraging to be able to speak for only ten minutes on a Bill that has such great implications for the future of our country, for the health of our economy, for our unemployed and all the other aspects. In the ten minutes allotted to me I will confine my remarks to two very important principles that we have to
May 7, 1984

look at in this Bill. The first is the matter of accountability; the second is the matter of fairness within the marketplace.
The Government wants to have us believe that Crown corporations will always be accountable, that they are accountable to Parliament, that their annual reports will be tabled in the House and therefore the committees of the House are free to examine those reports. That, in the definition of the Government, is accountability.
However, there are reasons why Crown corporations are increasingly unaccoutable to Parliament. The first reason for this is the massive proliferation of Crown corporations. Frankly, we are losing track of how many Crown corporations there are, where they are, what they are doing and even whether they still deserve to exist. The population explosion of Crown corporations is such that we really cannot keep track of which Crown corporations exist in the marketplace.
I listened with care to the remarks of my hon. friend from Rosedale who spoke last week. He was quoting the Auditor General's report and pointed out that the Auditor General has been concerned about the fact that in the past 22 years the number of Crown corporations has been increased by something like 300. In 1962, 22 years ago, about 28 Crown corporations were in existence; there are now over 300 Crown corporations in existence. Back in 1962, the existing Crown corporations had known assets of about $8.4 billion. Today, those assets are now in the neighbourhood of $74 billion with an additional $63 billion of liabilities. We must ask ourselves how we got from the situation which existed in 1962 when there were 28 Crown corporations to the situation which exists in 1984 when there are over 300 Crown corporations.
If Government Members would like to say that these Crown corporations are accountable to Parliament, all we need do is ask ourselves whether those of us who have been here for half of those 22 years have seen legislation enacting each one of those over 300 Crown corporations. The answer is a very simple no. Some parent Crown corporations have within their enabling legislation the right to spawn further Crown corporations. Therefore, it is almost impossible for us to keep track of which Crown corporations exist in the marketplace. There are very different pieces of legislation which enable the Crown corporations to do that.
Today we are debating the Financial Administration Act dealing with Crown corporations. The title of the legislation would lead the general public to believe that because we are dealing with a Bill with a title which includes Crown corporations, it is legislation which affects all Crown corporations. Nothing could be further from the truth, Mr. Speaker. I have received correspondence from a company called Canertech regarding a company in British Columbia which was formed under the Canada Business Corporations Act. I will refer to that company a little later on in my remarks. As well, companies have been spawned by the petroleum legislation which has been passed by the House. On and on it goes and we have simply lost track of them all.
Financial Administration Act
The second reason that there is no longer any real accountability and why there will be a diminishing level of accountability under this legislation is the shift of responsibility within Cabinet. In the parliamentary system of our country, Crown corporations have historically been accountable to the Minister to whom those Crown corporations report. That is eminently logical and I think the Canadian people generally believe that if a Crown corporation falls under the energy program, then the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) will be accountable for that corporation because it will report to that particular Minister. However, under the new legislation we are debating now, that will no longer necessarily be the case.
Accountability is now being shifted from the Minister to the Cabinet. It is being shifted from a specific responsibility to a general responsibility. How can accountability ever be demanded from a general body? I suppose the only way we could do so is to ask that general body to resign. I see that the Government is so interested in this legislation that the number of Members representing the Government who are present in the House has now been reduced to one. That tells us something about their level of interest. Responsibility is being shifted from the specific Minister to the entire Cabinet. No one will accept personal blame for the failure of any Crown corporation.
Another reason for the lack of accountability of Crown corporations is that Crown corporations enjoy a special and privileged position within the country under the terms assigned to them by the Government. My friend, the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn), in his brilliant remarks regarding the aspect of the responsibility and accountability of Crown corporations, pointed out that the uranium cartel was exempt from any kind of punishment. He pointed out that it was immune from prosecution. Any company in the marketplace must accept responsibility for its decisions. As pointed out by the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West, when Sears erred in its advertising, it had to pay $1 million. When the uranium cartel, under the protection of the Government, erred, it did not have to pay anything. It was exempt.
The second principle I would like to raise regarding the matter we are debating today is the principle of fairness in the marketplace. It seems to me that Crown corporations play a kind of schizophrenic role in the marketplace. As my colleague from Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) pointed out earlier, the general argument for establishing Crown corporations is that the marketplace is not meeting certain needs and therefore the Government must establish Crown corporations to meet those specific needs. Within the Canadian experience, none of us will argue that particular point of view. However, when a Crown corporation is purportedly founded to meet a need in the marketplace that is not otherwise being met, it at the same time wishes to argue that it is competing fairly and openly in the marketplace.
Nothing evidences that more clearly than the Federal Business Development Bank. It wants to say on the one hand that it is a bank of last resort meeting the needs of small businesses
3450

Financial Administration Act
in a way commercial banks do not, and on the other hand it wants to say that it is competing. It cannot have it both ways, Sir. Inevitably there is a conflict in goals. However, because of this privilege, Crown corporations enjoy a special relationship.
In the minute or two I have left, I would like to discuss the company to which I referred earlier, Canertech Inc. of Canada. That company sent out a news release some time ago announcing that Wood Gundy is conducting a survey of all energy companies in Canada and wants those companies to provide information to Canertech so that Canertech can help EMR provide an information base. To whom will that information base be provided? Will it be provided to companies like Pacific Enercon which exist to provide competition to private enterprise companies? The Government, by way of a Wood Gundy report, is seeking information from private companies in order to help government companies compete with private companies. That, Sir, creates unfairness in the marketplace.

Mr. Speaker, I wish I were able to conclude the comments of my hon. colleague. I too am pleased to rise to participate in the debate of this important Bill and this important subject and to face the problem of saying all I want to say about Crown corporations within a ten-minute time limit.
Bill C-24, known as the Crown corporations Bill, has been a long time in its making. The making of this Bill depicts the Government for what it is. It is flawed, ineffective and inoperative. Many here will recall that in 1979 the Progressive Conservative Government, in less than six months, introduced a Crown corporations Bill which followed very closely upon the very critical Lambert Commission report. We introduced that legislation so that it could be studied, improved and acted upon. But the Liberal-NDP coalition destroyed that opportunity. Almost five years later, the Government comes forward with this version of a Crown corporations Bill.
Quite frankly, Bill C-24 has virtually no chance of passing and receiving Crown approval, Royal Assent, during the present session. It has been introduced to deflect criticism of the fact that the Government has done nothing to rein in Crown corporations over the past five years. The last thing the Government wants is for the truth to come out about Cana-dair, de Havilland, Air Canada, the post office and a great number of other corporations already mentioned by my colleagues in their comments.
One way to keep the true story hidden is to introduce legislation at the last minute and then blame the Opposition for not passing it. We have a piece of legislation which promises much and delivers little. The issue is and clearly has been for several years that of accountability-accountability in, of and for Crown corporations.
Lawyers will always caution a client to read the fine print before a document or contract is signed. No lawyer would ever condone or recommend the signing of a contract before they saw or read the fine print. The kind of fine print we are talking about here is, of course, regulations. This Bill, with respect to almost every section of substance, allows the details to be written in later through regulations. Those regulations are subject to change at the whim of the responsible Minister.
Canadians may as well ask what the point of the legislation is if Crown corporations are going to be exempted from its provisions by regulation. It is worth noting as well that some 100 Crown corporations already in existence will not even be touched by this legislation. Their exemptions came early indeed. Neither does this Bill give Parliament any control over the creation of subsidiaries of Crown corporations, or the creation of a new or other subsidiary corporation where they are permitted in existing legislation. We will have proliferation in the growth of those corporations providing a safe sanctuary for retired or defeated Liberals in the years to come.
We on this side of the House have become increasingly annoyed by the growth of patronage appointments. Ability, competence and merit do not seem to matter any more. If there are not enough jobs to go around, the Government simply expands the creation of a good number of other sinecures.
This legislation would assist by redefining the board of directors of Crown corporations so that those boards would have a real and responsible purpose. In the private sector, the board of directors has a responsible chore; they have responsibility to the shareholders and to their directors. But here Cabinet would appoint the chief executive officer, set his tenure, fix his remuneration, and so it goes with the chairman of the board. The Cabinet would dictate dividend policy and, indeed, literally make all corporate decisions without the necessity of consulting with the board of directors affixed to that particular Crown corporation. What a farce! It is a long way around to provide a convenient resting place for government appointees.
It is interesting to note as well that Bill C-25, establishing the Canada Development Investment Corporation, allows the board of directors to appoint the chairman and the chief executive officer. Bill C-24 gives that responsibility to Cabinet. I am glad to see that there are now about five Government Members present. Confusion reigns on that side, as is so clearly evident among the present crop of leadership candidates.
Canadians are well familiar with the sinkhole some Crown corporations have become, filled in with taxpayers' money. The post office goes on losing hundreds of millions of dollars a year. VIA Rail is accomplishing the same feat. Canadair and de Havilland have shocked the nation through their losses. The Canadian taxpayer is left to wonder what really is going on in this Government. Someone has to be accountable for the excesses that have taken place. Accountability should be the cornerstone of any legislation dealing with Crown corporations. Government Members say "Trust us". The Government
May 7, 1984

record speaks for itself-Loto Canada, Petrofina and the election promise of "Elect us and the price of gasoline will go down". Bill C-24 is simply an open invitation to continue this Liberal tradition.
My constituents are well and truly fed up with newspaper headlines screaming about multimillion dollar losses by Crown corporations. Controls and accountability are a must. The Government has been promising action since 1977. If Bill C-24 is the best that the Government can do after seven years, then move over and let us take its place.

Mr. Speaker, like most Canadians I do not know a lot about Crown corporations, but I have a number of impressions in my mind and I have tried to rank them in what I consider some sort of order.
The first thing that comes to mind is that it appears there is a large number of Crown corporations which keep proliferating one after the other in leaps and bounds. In 1968 there were 38 Crown corporations; in 1980 there were 130, but there were 213 subsidiaries and 126 associate corporations. An example of how these corporations grew so fast is the Canada Lands Corporation which was formed in 1982. Since that time it has spawned five subsidiaries. It reminds me of asexual reproduction, where bacteria split in half and then those two halves split again and then split again. Before we know it, we have hundreds and hundreds of these corporations. The impression I get is that we do not know how many Crown corporations we have. We keep hearing that we have at least 400. I do not know if that is right or wrong, but I have never heard anyone stand up and tell us exactly how many Crown corporations there are in Canada.
Another impression I have is that Crown corporations continue to lose vast amounts of money. I am sure some of them probably make money, but we do not hear much about the ones that make money. We continue to hear about the huge sums of money that are poured into Crown corporations using taxpayers' dollars.
A third impression I have is that there is a vast build-up of debt charged to Crown corporations. Again, I have never seen a total or a figure. I have seen some figures, but I do not know how accurate they are. However, I do get the impression that there are billions and billions of dollars in debt piling up in Crown corporations.
The fourth impression I have is that there are a great man's people employed by Crown corporations. I believe I read one time that there were more people employed by Crown corporations than by the Public Service of the federal Government. That might not be accurate but it is the impression I have.
The fifth impression I have is that there is a problem with the auditing of Crown corporations as well as accountability and responsibility. When something goes wrong no one seems to be in charge. Everyone runs for cover. We do not know on whose desk the buck will finally wind up.
Financial Administration Act
The sixth impression I have is that many of the objectives of Crown corporations could be better served by the private sector.
Those are some of the impressions I have of Crown corporations and I dare say they are representative of what many Canadians think of Crown corporations. I apologize to Hon. Members for not having made an in-depth study of this subject and for not having more accurate knowledge. In any event, I felt when this Bill came forth that any thinking government would want to correct all of these impressions. Surely it would be an excellent plank on which to win an election.
Looking at Bill C-24, it appears that it is not what we had hoped it would be. There are many things which are left undone. For example, let me quote from the report of the Auditor General for 1982 with respect to accountability:
A major theme of my 1982 Annual Report was the accountability of Crown-owned corporations. With the exception of my predecessor's warnings about the state of government financial management in the mid-1970s, no issue involving my Office has captured more public attention than that of the accountability of these Crown-owned corporations. The reason is obvious. A lot of public money is at stake. The accountability framework for what I have referred to as this "sub-government" is inadequate.
On February 28 the Auditor General wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He was laudatory of the actions of the Prime Minister and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) for bringing forward this Bill. He said, and I quote:
I recollect that last June I wrote you, expressing my concerns about the need for a more effective accountability framework for Crown-owned corporations. I think it therefore only appropriate that I write again now when there is such tangible evidence of action that will help to alleviate my concerns.
May I be permitted to express my sincere thanks for the personal initiatives that you and members of your Cabinet have taken in this endeavour. I wish you and Mr. Gray smooth sailing in the House.
I do not think what the Auditor General really wanted is in this Bill. It seems as if there is much left to interpretation, and I do not believe it is very clear cut as to what the Auditor General's role is going to be as far as Crown corporations are concerned. I feel the Auditor General has settled for half a loaf and I wonder whether after hearing these debates over the past days, the Auditor General is still as satisfied with this legislation as he appeared to be in February.
As far as responsibility is concerned, Mr. Speaker, there is still no one responsible when it comes to this Bill. The Minister is certainly not responsible. It appears that the Cabinet is still taking the major role of responsibility and there are 30-odd Cabinet Ministers. Of course, as soon as they get into trouble, they are going to run for cover. I believe we are going to be in exactly the same position as we are at the moment. This Bill simply does not designate who is responsible when we get into a problem. Over and over in this Bill, Mr. Speaker, one sees that items are left to regulations and to discretion. That is simply not good enough when we are dealing with billions and billions of dollars and such a vast number of corporations. These things should be spelled out very definitely.
As far as the matter of proliferation is concerned, it seems as if an "end run" has been made around Parliament. Crown

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
corporations are still going to be able to spin off subsidiaries and that is where the real growth is going to occur. On top of that, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of other items which this Bill does not address, for instance, the privileges and immunities of Crown corporations. The matter of their immunity from the Combines Investigation Act has not been addressed in this Bill. The question of whether or not public servants should be allowed to sit on the boards of Crown corporations has not been addressed in this Bill, as well as the creation of any kind of parliamentary oversight committee, a watchdog type of thing for Crown corporations.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, the Bill is filled with half measures. It does not go as far as it should. It needs to be amended in many areas. As I said, I certainly do not profess to be any kind of an expert on Crown corporations, but I am unhappy with the Bill and I feel most thinking people in Canada would be as well. It is not a good enough Bill to correct the problems which Crown corporations have caused our country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today in opposition to Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations. I do not intend to go into this Bill clause by clause mainly because of lack of time. However, I will cover what I consider to be the most contentious parts of this particular Bill. I would first like to point out that the Bill is certainly not what the Government opposite purports it to be. Second, it is a travesty of errors and omission. It does nothing to change the present situation or the status quo regarding Crown corporations.
As a small-businessman, Mr. Speaker, I can tell you that the very survival of the day-to-day operations of my business relies mainly on accountability. That accountability, Mr. Speaker, I do not see in relationship to Crown corporations and this is what I feel Bill C-24 should provide. It should provide legislation which would demand this accountability, which would point out this accountability and enforce it.
Let me cover a few points related to this accountability factor. The Auditor General on numerous occasions has pointed out to the Government opposite the lack of accountability, but the Government opposite merely ignores it. I know the Auditor General can defend himself and does, but it should be pointed out that Bill C-24 just further neutralizes his position and Parliament's position.
I would like to dwell now on some of the more direct issues and why we in the Opposition oppose Bill C-24 in its present state. I take the example of Crown corporations such as de Havilland and Canadair. Most Canadians who look at these corporations see the financial disaster of the century. Canadian tax dollars have been, and continue to be, sunk into these sinking ships. Government approaches these corporations on a hit and miss basis, Mr. Speaker. The dollars which these corporations have swallowed up would have saved most of the small businesses which went bankrupt in 1982.
We are given the story that we are maintaining our technology by these investments. There is no one in this House,
Mr. Speaker, who wishes to preserve technology more than we do. But at what cost? Not at the cost of national bankruptcy, Mr. Speaker. We as a Party and myself as an individual have spoken many times in this House on unemployment. I realize the importance of the jobs in these two Crown corporations, and I will do what I can to protect those jobs, as will other Hon. Members of my Party. However, we are jeopardizing these jobs, instead of protecting them, through a lack of accountability.
I would now like to look at Cabinet's role regarding Bill C-24. How does Cabinet deal with the disastrous performance of these Crown corporations? Do they bring in meaningful reform? Absolutely not, Mr. Speaker. Instead, this Bill gives more control to Cabinet. Cabinet is supposed to be running this country and every economic indicator shows it is having a great deal of difficulty. Its members should spend their time running the country instead of trying to run these Crown corporations. Just as a personal observation, as a small-businessman I would not hire one of the members of the present Government to run or oversee any of my businesses, not even a peanut stand. Therefore, why should we give them this ultimate power under Bill C-24?
Under this Bill, Mr. Speaker, the Cabinet would acquire much greater authority to overrule a board of directors. It could appoint a board and then overrule them before they start. It can deny information to Parliament without explanation. In this its members are consistent, Mr. Speaker: they operate as a democratic dictatorship; they exempt certain Crown corporations from general provisions of the Bill. If Cabinet wants to have a sideline, start a little gimmick, the provisions are there. It can fine-tune the application of the Bill by making regulations that need not be disclosed to Parliament. That is what the Cabinet is responsible for, Mr. Speaker, not disclosing to Parliament what it should. These are clear impediments to accountability and I fear the result will be the inefficient running of Crown corporations.
The Cabinet adopted auditing methods such that Liberal-appointed patronage auditors will audit the performance of Liberal-appointed executives of these corporations, supervised by a Liberal Cabinet. This is like taking all the foxes and putting them in with the chickens. It is bad enough that Canadian taxpayers have to subsidize the fees and salaries of these patronage appointees, but must they pay the bill for their mismanagement?
What is Bill C-24 really? I suggest it is ominous, creeping socialism. The Liberal appointees go to the boards, collect their honorariums and do what the Government tells them to do. Cabinet appoints the vice-presidents of some Crown corporations such as Canada Post and CMHC, and then appoints the auditors. It makes and approves the by-laws and sets the dividend policy. If the vice-president, the auditor and the board of directors are all appointed by Cabinet, there is a conflict of interest. But they would not understand conflict of interest because that is the way they operate. No one in Crown
May 7, 1984

corporations will speak out for fear of losing their jobs, so the losses continue to grow. Even if they do speak out, the Government says nothing. The Cabinet makes the final decision.
There must be individual ministerial responsibility, Mr. Speaker, but this Bill places responsibility with groups of Ministers. That is one reason these Crown corporations have staggering losses which continue to grow. I cannot repeat often enough that accountability is the problem, not reorganization through CDIC and super-Crown corporations which will only result in greater mismanagement and greater dollar losses.
Yesterday I listened to the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston). The questions he raises concerning the money lost in Crown corporations are serious. The losses are horrendous. When we see the tragedy and despair of youth unemployment, the opportunity cost of that money is unforgivable; this from a senior Minister in the Government. Mr. Speaker, nothing this Government does can be viewed in isolation. Money lost by Crown corporations means less money for medicare, education and reforestation, to name just a few. This Bill does not address the problems facing this country. We will continue to slide backwards economically if we do not change this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, unlike most of my colleagues I do not intend to deal with what Bill C-24 does, even though what it does is inadequate or wrong. Instead, I would like to focus on some of the many important issues with which, to my mind, Bill C-24 should deal but does not.
Contrary to what we have heard from the Government, this Bill is not an ambitious piece of legislation in any way, shape or form. It really does not cover anything new. Many of these issues have already received a great deal of public notice. For example, they have been covered in a series of reports from the Auditor General dating back to 1976. Some of these issues were canvassed in the blue book published by the Privy Council Office in 1977. Some were reviewed in the Estey Commission of Inquiry into Air Canada. They have been covered in the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, particularly the Crown corporations report of 1978. They were studied extensively by the Lambert Commission in its 1979 report. Some of these issues were the subject of Bill C-27, the omnibus Crown corporations Bill formulated and tabled by the short-lived Progressive Conservative Clark Government in 1979.
I am disappointed in this Bill before us today because I do not think it really breaks any new ground at all. It is simply a haphazard amalgamation of selected recommendations, observations and reforms from a host of previous studies, reports and Bills. I suppose one reason Bill C-24 lacked any apparent over-all consistency is that the Government has chosen a set of supposed solutions without any attempt at overall rationality. I do not think the Government can make up its mind on what it really wants to do with Crown corporations. For example, why is this Bill in conflict or inconsistent in so many respects with
Financial Administration Act
the specific Crown corporation Bill, Bill C-25, dealing with the CDIC?
I have indicated that I want to talk about what Bill C-24 does not even purport to do, Mr. Speaker. First, a Bill such as this, which is long overdue, provides a wonderful opportunity for the Government to wind up several Crown corporations which are inactive, some of which have been inactive for some time. I have in mind companies such as Canadian National (West Indies) Steamships Ltd., Loto Canada Incorporated, Uranium Canada Limited and others. It would have been good management, something which is apparently foreign to the Government, to wind up these corporations.
In addition, such a move would have prohibited the Government from reactivating these corporations at a future date as the public Works Land Company was in 1978, after a long period of inactivity, to administer the lands peripheral to Mirabel Airport. The reason such an old and dead Crown corporation was reactivated was to enable the Government to avoid any scrutiny or control by Parliament. Instead, the Government has added many of these inactive corporations to the schedules of Bill C-24. I hope you will forgive me Mr. Speaker, for suspecting that this is intentional and that the motivations are anything but honourable.
Second, Mr. Speaker, Crown corporations enjoy a long list of privileges and immunities by virtue of their ownership by the Crown. These are privileges and immunities not enjoyed by their private sector competitors. Bill C-24 says nothing about those privileges and immunities. For instance, when borrowing on the capital markets, many Crown corporations enjoy "sovereign status" and their rating and cost of money or, in other words, their interest, is roughly equal to that of the Government of Canada.
Most Crown corporations are immune to a wide range of federal and provincial statutes. As we saw in the uranium cartel case, for example, Eldorado Nuclear in my own constituency and Uranium Canada were held to be immune from the federal Government's Combines Investigation Act. That is certainly an inequitable position which should be dealt with in a comprehensive Bill such as this. Under the current Patent Act, most Crown corporations have full and unrestricted access to Canadian patents without the payment of royalties or fees.
I will not go on, Mr. Speaker. Time does not permit me to list the full range of privileges and immunities enjoyed by Crown corporations. The private sector has asked the Government again and again to remove at least some of these privileges and immunities from those Crown corporations which compete with private sector enterprises. Bill C-24 says nothing about that.
Third, Mr. Speaker, Section 45 of the Financial Administration Act provides that the borrowings of agent Crown corporations are to be recorded as direct liabilities against the federal Government's Consolidated Revenue Fund. Instead, the Government has engaged in an accounting sleight of hand by

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
recording such borrowings as contingent liabilities, thereby understating the Government's gross direct financial exposure. The accounting community, the Auditor General and the financial markets of Canada have repeatedly asked the Government to straighten out this situation by either having the accounting practices reflect the law or the law reflect the accounting practice. If the Government had the courage of its convictions, it would have set the record straight one way or the other. Instead, Bill C-24 says absolutely nothing about this.
Fourth, Crown corporations are usually heavily debt financed. This practice too allows the Government to engage in some accounting manoeuvrability. As the Public Accounts Committee noted, the debt financing of the Canadair Challenger and the de Havilland Dash programs not only represented poor business judgment, but was also responsible in part for those companies' current chaotic financial situation. Debt financing makes it more difficult to compare the performance of Crown corporations with that of private sector competitors. Debt financing helps to keep Crown corporations tied to the public trough. Debt financing makes Crown corporations more susceptible to interest rate fluctuations and economic downturns. Again, Bill C-24 does absolutely nothing about this.
In many other ways which I have not had time to discuss, Sir, Bill C-24 should be drastically amended before it goes through the House.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the discussion on Bill C-24 in relation to Crown corporations. I would like to begin by saying that two separate and extremely critical issues have become the trademark of the Trudeau times. I am speaking primarily for all of western Canada. First, there is the ever-increasing budget deficit. Second, there is the irresponsible management and lack of accountability of Crown corporations. Bill C-24 concerns the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations.
In my own constituency I have found that Crown corporations are always the subject of critical comment. Perhaps this is due to a number of reasons. People are always poorly informed about Crown corporations. They never seem to be able to learn details such as why they exist in the first place and how long they might be expected to operate. Crown corporations are difficult for any politician to explain because in many cases they seem to serve such a nebulous purpose. They are also difficult to explain because there are so many Crown corporations in existence and they are so variable in their operations.
A few examples come to my mind from personal experience in my constituency. The one which is by far the easiest to recall is Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada operates a number of producing gas wells and pipelines on my cattle ranch in southeastern Alberta and has for a number of years. Petro-Canada did not explore and discover this gas field; it was purchased with taxpayers' money. That makes a tremendous difference in the feeling towards Petro-Canada in the western part of Canada, especially in the gas-producing area of the
southern Prairies. In the case at hand Petro-Canada purchased its assets from Atlantic Richfield Canada Limited. The first visible result of this takeover was a marked increase in the number of employees and the number of trucks used to tear around the country in. At the same time there was a marked decrease in gas well drilling activities. Petro-Canada is the most visible evidence and reminder of the National Energy Program. This Program is still considered to be a total disaster in western Canada, especially in the last three years.
Further evidence of this disaster has been the collapse of the oil and gas well servicing industry centered around Brooks and Medicine Hat in southern Alberta. Brooks was a thriving small town. It has tripled its population in a very short period of time, due mainly to the interest in gas well servicing. Brooks had attained a population of about 9,000. Now it is a veritable ghost town. This is because of the harsh reaction of the National Energy Program and its backlash on the oil and gas wells, especially the gas well servicing industry.
There is now no evidence of a recovery in the natural gas industry in western Canada and there will be none until the export of natural gas from the southern Prairies to the United States picks up significantly. The only hope for better days in our natural gas industry in Alberta is increased gas export to the United States.
The most knowledgeable people in this field now indicate that that pick-up cannot be expected for two or three years. The only way there will be an increase in activity in our natural gas industry is by significant gas export increases to the United States.
There is another, totally different type of Crown corporation about which I want to comment. That is Canagrex. It is still a bitter memory for many of us. Presumably the Canagrex operation is now in place but there is no report of any real activities in finding any new markets for our agricultural products. Rather, just the opposite is taking place right now, especially in my own industry, the beef cattle industry. Other countries are now finding new markets here in Canada. Just last week, during the NDP opposition day when they were debating agriculture, the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) was the second speaker. He drew attention to the two-way trade between some European Economic Community countries and Canada. Without going into detail, he gave me an opportunity to remind the Minister about excessive beef imports now coming in from such countries as the Republic of Ireland, Denmark and Holland. In the case of the Republic of Ireland, its beef is being imported into Canada presently with an import subsidy by Ireland of 50 cents a pound in Canadian currency. The same situation is occurring with canned pork from Denmark.
Our Canadian cattle producers, specifically the Canadian Cattlemen's Association, reminded both the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Regan) of this situation three months ago. At that time the cattle producers asked for countervailing duties to be imposed
May 7, 1984

at the same amount of money that the import subsidies from the countries in Europe amounted to. Yet nothing has been done about this by either Minister to date. They have suggested that perhaps the whole situation should be investigated even further.
Very briefly, I want to comment on the post office in my own community. Our first-class mail takes much too long to be delivered. I speak with personal knowledge and I am referring only to western Canada. The post office facilities in Medicine Hat, especially for customer parking, are terrible. If we as Members of Parliament in the west had to depend totally on our post office for our constituency communication, our whole system would have collapsed long ago. The saving feature for all of us, of course, is the excellent telephone service that we are provided with and allowed to use extensively.
I want to conclude by referring to the excellent speech that opened this whole debate. It was made by our spokesman, the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson). He said as reported at page 2385 of Hansard:
-we will never solve the problems of Crown corporations until they come under an effective regime of individual ministerial accountability-
Bill C-24 goes in the opposite direction. The individual Minister is nothing but a post box-
The real authority is, of course, exercised by Cabinet or Treasury Board; groups of Ministers rather than individuals. In being accountable to so many Ministers, corporations will continue to be accountable to no one.

Mr. Speaker, the question of Crown corporations has been before the Canadian people for approximately 70 years. We are still faced with the same problem, which is that of accountability.
This Bill involves a simple vote to send this new effort on the part of the Government to a committee. I am saying in all seriousness that it is the most useless action that anyone could think of. The committee will discuss this issue at length and arrive at no decision.
Let me give the House some simple advice. If this House wishes to serve the country, let us abandon this Bill. We know that there is a dying government which has no intention of returning this Bill to the House in this session. Let this legislation disappear so that we can have a chance to spend two or three years to get at the basic problem.
My own positive contribution to the debate would be to suggest that one provision in particular should be included in any Bill dealing with the accountability of Crown corporations if it is to succeed. My advice simply is that if accountability is turned over to the Cabinet, as this Bill does, the same mistakes will be made as have been made during the last 70 years.
This subject was discussed in great detail during the period 1964 to 1967. At that time we were debating one of the biggest Crown corporations in Canada, Canadian National Railways, within the debate of the whole national transportation Bill. Members of the House discussed this at great length and I believe close to 70 amendments came from the floor of the House of Commons. All but two of those amendments were accepted by the Government.
It is interesting to note what those two exceptions were. One amendment concerned the question of accountability. I will not go through the whole debate at that time because it is not necessary. The Official Opposition made that recommendation about accountability but it was turned down by the Government and the NDP. subtopic: EXTENSION OF BENEFITS URGED FOR ATLANTIC FISHERMEN
EXTENSION OF BENEFITS URGED FOR ATLANTIC FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the House the disastrous situation on the northeast coast of Newfoundland and in many areas of Atlantic Canada because of the incredible amount of ice located along the coastline of most of our Atlantic provinces. subtopic: AMENDMENT SOUGHT OF SECTION AFFECTING FARMERS
AMENDMENT SOUGHT OF SECTION AFFECTING FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Section 31 of the Income Tax Act has been plaguing farmers for over 20 years. Finally, in a token reaction to public pressure, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) announced on February 15 that he was going to set up a consultative group to look into the matter. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is two and one-half months later and the Minister has not yet even named the members of this group.
In that two and one-half month interval, Revenue Canada could conceivably reassess a farmer, turn down his notice of objection, and garnishee his bank account. In other words, in
that period of time Revenue Canada could bankrupt a farmer. Recently, in a ten-week period, the Progressive Conservative Party announced its Revenue Canada task force, conducted public hearings in 23 Canadian centres, and drafted and submitted an 80-page report, in both official languages, covering all areas of the Department's operations.
It appears as if the Section 31 problem has been put on the Liberal back burner. Who knows how much more time will be spent studying the issue and providing recommendations to say nothing of the interval the Government will take to act upon those suggestions? At the speed the Liberal Government is going, it will be another 20 years before this stupid and destructive Section of the Income Tax Act is amended.
Fortunately, it is more likely that the consultative group will be reporting to a Conservative Government, and farmers can rest assured that immediate action will be taken.
