subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT RECONSIDER AID PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the last report of the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association showed that the total value of shipyard production dropped 38 per cent in 1983, compared with 1982. It seems that the industry is suffering as a result of imports of ships into Canada.
Recent measures announced by the federal Government are aimed at helping the industry. First of all, federal orders have been a godsend, because they represent 80 per cent of new orders received this year. Second, there is Bill C-16, that extends the customs zone to the edge of the continental shelf. However, I feel that this is not enough. I do not think the reasons for exempting fishing boats of between 30 and 50 metres from the provisions of Bill C-16 are very convincing. Furthermore, the Petroleum Incentives Program makes it possible to pay 80 per cent of oil exploration costs to Canadian drilling companies. I have nothing against this measure, except that it should apply only to what is produced in Canada.
I therefore urge the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to reconsider this part of the Energy Program and I also hope that the Shipbuilding Industry Assistance Program will be extended until June 30, 1987, because I feel it is hardly appropriate to terminate this program at a time when Canadian shipyards are in great difficulty.

subtopic: "THE SAGA OF SAHARA SAM"-NEED FOR GOOD MANAGEMENT
"THE SAGA OF SAHARA SAM"-NEED FOR GOOD MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about a hundred years ago a scrawny little fellow named Sam showed up in an Ottawa Valley lumber camp. He asked for a job as a faller.
The boss reluctantly hired him, but was completely flabbergasted at the end of the day when he saw how many trees Sam had fallen. "Where did you learn to fall trees?" he asked. "In the Sahara", said Sam. "Go on, there aren't any trees in the Sahara," said the boss. "There aren't now," said Sam.
Sahara Sam finished his work in the Ottawa Valley and moved on to British Columbia, where he has been busy ever since.
This is National Forestry Week and it would be a good time for the federal Government to start taking seriously our forests and our forest industry, before our forests become desert.
Across Canada we harvest more than 800,000 hectares of forest each year, but 25 per cent to 50 per cent of that land is never regenerated, or it grows up in non-commercial species.
The Canadian Forest Service estimates that decent forest management would create 100,000 new jobs, increase product sales by $22 billion, increase exports by $12 billion, and generate an additional $3 billion in tax revenues.
If the Government gave proper attention to the needs of the Canadian people and to the needs of our economy-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been impressed by the efforts of an organization in my riding called AEDA, the acronym for "Against Easy Divorce Association". Their concern is the deleterious effect that so-called "no-fault" divorce can have on the children of couples whose marriage ends in divorce.
This group points out that 40 per cent of all Canadian children of divorced couples live in single parent homes. The lifestyle of the children of divorced parents changes rapidly. The children are placed under social assistance rather than cared for by non-custodial parents or, if the custodial parent, usually the mother, works, the children for the most part are left without necessary parental supervision during their developing years.
Added to these indignities, children from easy or no-fault divorces are generally confused as to the reasons why their
parents have split up, and children have not understood, even years later, why their parents' marriage ended. Indeed, there may be a link between the rising suicide rate, particularly among young people, and their growing suspicion and distrust of the actions of their parents. As far as children are concerned, their parents remain married forever. AEDA is correct. Too easy divorce can have serious consequences for children as well as for others indirectly involved.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday the Supreme Court of Canada, in a unanimous decision, ruled that Newfoundland's Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act was ultra vires. This legislation was passed in 1980 in an attempt to redress one of the most serious grievances in this country today, that is, the Churchill Falls power contract. The contract entered into in 1969 by Churchill Falls Power Corporation and Hydro Quebec locks Newfoundland into a situation whereby Churchill Falls power is sold to Quebec for less than three mills. That power is resold to the Americans, and indeed to other Canadian provinces, for up to 28 mills. In dollars, according to the Economic Council of Canada, this means $8 million a year for Newfoundland, and $800 million a year for Quebec.
This country cannot survive on a strict interpretation of the letter of the law. There has to be a spirit of the law. It is in that spirit that I call upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on behalf of the people of Newfoundland, to take whatever steps are available to him under the National Energy Program, or through amendments to the National Energy Program, to correct this most grave injustice. Failure to do so could have most dire consequences.

subtopic: REDRESS SUGGESTED FOR JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
REDRESS SUGGESTED FOR JAPANESE CANADIANS INTERNED DURING WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of their history most countries make mistakes which subsequent leaders are required to acknowledge and rectify. Such is the case today with respect to the treatment of our fellow Canadians of Japanese descent during World War II. The people who were unilaterally uprooted and forcibly relocated, and whose boats, farms, and possessions were expropriated, with very little and often no compensation, were full Canadian citizens. They were Canadians in all respects, and deserved all the protection that citizenship implies.
They were hard-working, lawful, and paid taxes like all other Canadians. Not one Canadian of Japanese descent was

May 7, 1984
ever convicted of an act of disloyalty toward this country. The Government reacted to unsubstantiated fears and hatred. I call upon the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to reconsider the position of his Government and to set in motion immediately the proper process to address and deal with this serious issue.

Mr. Speaker, one of the most deadly toxics known to man is 2, 3, 7, 8, -dioxin, dangerous traces of which found their way into 2, 4, 5, -T and the Agent Orange mixture that has been used as a herbicide in Canada. The severe damage caused by the compound 2, 3, 7, 8, -dioxoin came to light during the Vietnam War, and now further revelations have come out in the multi-billion dollar lawsuit taken against chemical manufacturers by thousands of former army servicemen. We also knew that Dow Chemical knew as early as 1965 that this deadly dioxin was finding its way into herbicide products in Canada, but to protect its lucrative sales in our country this evidence was kept quiet for five years.
The Government has done nothing to date to protect our citizens from the harmful effects of dioxins like 2, 3, 7, 8. The Government takes the position that all chemicals are safe unless proven otherwise. As the IBT scandal revealed, the Government relies on the bogus reports of the chemical manufacturers to trumpet safety claims to the Canadian people. We still continue the use of 2, 4, 5, -T which the United States banned in 1969. We know that deadly dioxins are seeping into Canada from old American waste dumps, but still the Government does nothing.
In conclusion, responsibility for pesticides and herbicides must be removed from Agriculture Canada. A special task force on pesticides and toxic waste must be established to tour the country and bring in a set of hard-hitting regulations for the future, and a serious plan for past errors. Corporate executives must be held legally liable for violations. A beefed up program to research and develop natural alternatives to toxic chemicals must be put into high gear.

subtopic: FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR AIRPORT COMPLETION IN GRENADA
FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE FOR AIRPORT COMPLETION IN GRENADA
speechtext:

In my riding, where unemployment has reached 47 per cent, crisis proportions, the same can be said of the need to complete an airport. What are the Government's priorities?

As far as the question itself is concerned, I want to remind my friend that, indeed, the issue of an artificial ceiling on interest rates was extensively studied at the time when the Bank Act to which he referred was revised.
This issue has been studied extensively over and over again, repeatedly, every time that interest rates tend to go up. All those who have studied this subject have come to the conclusion that it is wrong to set some artificial ceilings on interest rates, for the good reason that the net result in the end tends to be that funds going into that area end up being very limited and there is not enough to meet the demand. I believe, therefore, this country would be much better served-

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CEILING ON MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext: By driving people out of their homes.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR CEILING ON MORTGAGE INTEREST RATES
speechtext: -by relying on the rules of the market and trying to keep interest rates as low as we can, generally, to all Canadians, whether they want to buy a home, farm, small business, or borrow to buy a car or some appliances. I believe that the best solution remains one whereby the consumers will have the choice to allocate their borrowings according to their needs, rather than making the artificial decision for them.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. The Minister will know that rising mortgage interest rates are of continuing concern to the Canadian home owner and the housing industry. Last week the Minister assured the House that everyone who has taken out a mortgage since March 1 will be eligible for the mortgage interest insurance protection plan. In the absence of the legislation, which has been promised for almost two months now, can the Minister explain to the House just what that eligibility is going to mean to the average Canadian home owner?

Mr. Speaker, I have indicated that we have proceeded with extensive consultations with the housing and construction industry, as well as consumer groups, and that those consultations have been concluded. We should be able to introduce a Bill by the end of this month which I hope will receive prompt consideration by the House.
As to the nature of the proposal, I have indicated that all home buyers since March 1, 1984, would be eligible for the program and, second, I released at the time of the Budget an extensive document which provided for the nature of this particular program, to which I invite my friend to refer.
I must say that the consultations we have had, which have been quite extensive across Canada, have indicated very broad support for the measure we have put forward, and it is

expected that the Bill to be introduced will be substantially along the lines of what was proposed in the Budget.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the Minister that the problem will not be with the concept but with the mechanics.

Mr. Speaker, we have been calling on the Government to open its eyes and stop squandering billions of dollars in an area which has produced nothing but dry holes. Finally, I am amazed that the Hon. Member wants to put forward as a philosophy or policy in the energy field the idea that we should go only for wells which will produce. The history of the oil and gas sector is one of a large number of dry holes, with a few discoveries. If you want to have discoveries you have to drill, and you will not be successful most of the time. You will be successful a number of times, and this is how the industry has developed in Canada and around the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I begin by thanking the Hon. Member for his question. As he knows, the Pension Act establishes the process by which entitlement to disability pensions is determined. It is a quasi-judicial process and was developed by veterans to serve veterans. Over the past couple of years we have taken steps to speed up the administrative process by which veterans' applications for disability pensions are handled. We have not, however, looked at the basis for the adjudication process under the Pension Act.
I have taken action not only to meet with the War Amps of Canada and their representative, Mr. Chadderton, a couple of weeks ago, but I further examined whether or not the adjudication process continues to meet the needs of veterans in the 1980s. May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet (for Mr. Gray) that Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned at one o'clock, I was laying down the background for a positive proposal to be made with respect to any legislation dealing with Crown corporations under the Financial Administration Act. I pointed out this morning that this is not a new subject and that efforts were made some 15 years ago to give the House some form of responsibility for the accountability work that must be done with these Crown corporations. We are dealing with the same suggestions 15 years later.
When one examines this Bill more closely, it is evident that accountability will be given to the cabinet. All common sense dictates that since the Cabinet has enough to do, it will delegate that responsibility to civil servants who will oversee the accountability of other civil servants. In effect, the same mistakes that have been made over the last 70 years are being repeated.
The one positive suggestion whose precedents I believe made it workable was that suggestion made in the House approximately 15 years ago by the Member for Peace River at that time, Ged Baldwin. I seconded that motion and I believe we made a fairly good argument for it. However, it was turned down by the Government and the NDP. They argued quite sincerely and honestly that if this power was given to civil servants they should be trusted and permitted to run the corporation as they saw fit. This willy-nilly type of thinking has proven to be a disaster.
I put my proposal forward quite seriously in the hope that, if this legislation goes to committee, a suggestion will be made to remove the proposal that accountability be put into the hands of the Cabinet. I suggest that that is a useless form of accountability. My proposal is to use the experience of the Australian Parliament where important subjects in that country are referred to a statutory committee as distinct from the ordinary standing committee that we have. The statutory committee meets automatically and draws its power from Parliament and is not subject to the whims of Cabinet. Such a committee is comparable to the Public Accounts Committee in our country. However, this statutory committee includes competent people who work for the parliamentary committee and who can scrutinize these Crown corporations that are made accountable to the committee. While this cannot be done for all Crown corporations, I certainly believe that the major
Crown corporations should be under some form of statutory committee.
Another precedent that I wanted to mention comes from the Province of Saskatchewan. When the CCF first came to power in 1944, the Province of Saskatchewan had a large number of Crown corporations. That legislature took an important step in appointing a Committee of the Whole House to scrutinize Crown corporations. However, one of the regulations in that provision was that the legislature itself could not adjourn until that committee was satisfied that it had received all of the information it required from a particular Crown corporation. When the Crown corporation civil servants realized that they would be kept there until they answered, they would provide the information. That was a successful form of accountability which even led in some cases to dismissal and reprimands to those in charge.
I can give further examples but I believe I have made it quite clear that a positive suggestion for this legislation is that accountability not be put into the hands of people who are too busy and unable to carry it out. This pertains to a single Minister, as we discovered with Transport, or to the Cabinet as a whole.
I believe that a committee working full time, completely independent from Cabinet and whose recommendations Parliament must heed, would be able to act on the recommendations or warnings of the Auditor General before they are two years too late.
I suggest these views are held by many people in the civil service. Let me quote from a report which I do not believe was ever made public. It was given as a seminar paper to the Canadian Transportation Commission some nine years ago and was written by one of the last old-fashioned mandarins who believed in giving honest judgment and advice.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-24 before us today is an important Bill to amend the Financial Administration Act as it pertains to Crown corporations. The legislation, I am afraid, is a great deal of smoke and mirrors. What this legislation reflects is the concern which the Liberal Government has now about the public's attention to and its suspicion of those Crown corporations which the Liberals set up. This Bill reflects a mechanism which the Liberal Government is hoping to use in an election campaign to indicate to the public that there is concern among the caucus and the Cabinet. As a result the Government through this Bill is going to deflect some of the anger, frustration and bewilderment which the public presently has toward Crown corporations, Crown corporations which Canadians do accept and do understand are a part of the mixed economy we have and have had for some time.
The public is concerned over the revelations about Canadair and de Havilland and the massive debt those corporations have accumulated over the past few years. People are concerned that the Government did not seem to understand that these corporations were running up large deficits until it was revealed that Canadair had a deficit of $1.4 billion. The public is concerned that Canada Post Corporation has not met the level of efficiency expected. Everybody has examples of mail service inefficiency, examples of letters being lost or mail misplaced for months and months.
Then there is the concern about Petro-Canada, a corporation set up with a great deal of public support. Indeed, this was a corporation which the pbulic hoped would be a window on the oil industry. But we are finding that the public is becoming very disenchanted with Petro-Canada, and I think rightfully so. Petro-Canada is operatinmg much like any other corporation in the oil industry, in a great deal of secrecy, with very little public input in terms of the service people can expect of it, its pricing policies and access to information about its financial position and the investments in which Petro-Canada is involved.
This legislation is really an appeal to the public in an election period. If we look at some of the terminology in the press release of the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) announcing the legislation, we cannot argue with its intent. What do we have? We find terminology to the effect that Crown corporations should become more accountable to the public, that Crown corporations should operate under sound management procedures. A Crown corporation should produce a mandate for the pbulic and Parliament to understand what it intends to do, plans should be filed, and the objectives should all be placed before Parliament and government. All of these terms are commendable and supportable. There is a little bit of suspicion, particularly on my part, that we are getting into legislation which does not meet all those criteria, as with much of the legislation which the Liberal Government passes.
Financial Administration Act
Why have these policies not been implemented in the past? Why do we wait until this particular time? Every Crown corporation should be operating under sound management. The public should be aware of the mandate and the objectives of a Crown corporation. We have waited until 1984 because it has been divulged that the public mood toward Crown corporations is changing.
In terms of this legislation, I wonder whether we have the resources in Parliament and in the provincial legislatures to deal with the number of Crown corporations that have been set up. In Schedules B and C, for example, there are some 50 Crown corporations listed. These Crown corporations have some 129 subsidiaries. They have assets of some $47 billion and employ 209,000 people. That covers only the 50 corporations and their subsidiaries; there are far more Crown corporations than that. The kind of mechanism proposed in this legislation does not give us the opportunity to deal with those Crown corporations and their function adequately without some kind of parliamentary assistance.
In the short time I have left, Mr. Speaker, I want to talk about the fishing industry. My Conservative colleagues are somewhat critical of the number of Crown corporations there are, I think rightfully so. We have to assess the value of those corporations. I know that in the fishing industry we have a number of Crown corporations. In Schedule C, for example, we find the Canadian Fisheries Products Company, the Canadian Saltfish Corporation, the Fishwater Fish Marketing Corporation and the St. Anthony Fisheries Limited. These corporations were not set up particularly because government wanted to get into the processing sector of fishing industry. All of these corporations were set up because the private sector was unable to operate effectively and efficiently in the fishing industry whether on the Prairies through the Freshwater Fish Marketing Coporation or in Atlantic Canada through the Saltfish Corporation. These companies were set up by the Government in order to protect jobs in the communities, those jobs benefited and the fishermen who were dependent on one of the only resources in the northern parts of the provinces of Saskatchewan or Manitoba, or on the East Coast. Those corporations are serving public policy and those communities. They will continue to serve them because the private sector could not function or support those industries themselves.
However, if we look at the restructuring of the Atlantic fishery, we get an indication of how the Government really feels about accountability and openness in Crown corporations. We passed a Bill restructuring the Atlantic fishery in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. That Bill was expected to be passed within a couple of days effecting an expenditure of $138 million. Parliament was not given adequate financial information concerning that restructuring, a restructuring that put massive amounts of Canadian funds into the Atlantic fishery. That is not accountability as far as this Parliament is concerned.
If we are to have accountability, there must be some initiative on the part of the Government to provide Parliament and its members with adequate information to make decisions

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
about Crown corporations. I have some suspicion that that will not happen. When we see a major restructuring with a day long debate in committee and without adequate access, how are we expected as Members of Parliament to deal with the hundreds and hundreds of Crown corporations if there is not that sincerity, accountability and the willingness on the part of the Government to allow Members of Parliament to look at the financial structure of Crown corporations, particularly in the commercial field? Without sincerity and accountability, Members of Parliament will not achieve anything more through this legislation than they have under the present legislation.
With that in mind, I think we have to be convinced that the Government, through legislation and some amendments to this present Bill, will really allow Members of Parliament and this House to have the information to make the directors of the Crown corporations accountable to the Canadian public.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this important and utterly inadequate Bill before us, C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act in relation to Crown corporations, I must admit to a continuing sense of bewilderment about the business of this House. I know that I have been a Member of this Chamber long enough that nothing should surprise me, but it does. I cannot overcome the Alice in Wonderland sense of disorientation in which this Government seems to fulfil its legislative obligations.
Here we have a Bill which supposedly will restore accountability to the management of our Crown corporations. According to its sponsors, Ministers of the Crown will be responsible for these corporations and they will have the duty of reporting to Parliament. At exactly the same time that these proposals come before us, we have the spectacle of the Crown corporation de Havilland paying unheard of bonuses to its executives for the sterling job of having lost $236 million. Ministers of the Crown have been more than rigorous in defence of these bonuses.
At the same time we have the spectacle-the word "spectacle" hardly does the phenomenon credit-of Liberal leadership candidates and Cabinet Ministers criss-crossing the country, disavowing any personal responsibility for the unholy mess they collectively have made of our economy. I need hardly reiterate for this House the flabbergasting performance of the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development (Mr. Johnston) just this past weekend. Whom are we to believe? Who truly speaks for the Government? The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) who, in introducing it, expounded that this Bill would clarify the responsibilities and relationships of Crown corporations and Ministers? Is it the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) who has no nobly defended de Havilland and CDIC bonuses? Is it the Minister for Economic Development who would have us believe the question is really academic since he will be cutting these Crown corporations loose just as soon as the June
convention is concluded? Whose voice is the voice of authority? It is like the old game show, "To tell the truth"? Is it Minister number one, Minister number two or Minister number three? The only difference is that on the game show you eventually found out who was telling the truth.
My colleagues who have spoken on this Bill have outlined thoroughly and convincingly why this Bill is so inadequate. In particular, the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) did so in his rebuttal to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) who spoke on behalf of the President of the Treasury Board. My colleague showed the many ways in which this Bill is deficient in the purpose for which it was intended; the subsidiaries of Crown corporations which are exempt from the control of Parliament, all 150 or so of them, the built-in closure to cut off debate on the creation of a new Crown corporation after only seven hours and 30 days in committee, and the possible power of the Governor in Council to by pass Parliament altogether in creating new corporations.
To be sure, Bill C-24 promises regulations to make Crown corporations accountable to Parliament, but it does not specify what those regulations are to be. What we have is a set of conditions and circumstances in which such regulations may be suspended or even subverted entirely by the removal of a given Crown corporation from one schedule to another. Is it any wonder that we on this side of the House must treat this Bill with suspicion? Is it any wonder we question the accountability of Crown corporations under this Bill when the Bill itself so obscures the process of accountability as to make it invisible?
Under this Bill, boards of directors have no authority but to act as a rubber stamp. Cabinet picks the chairman and the chief executive officers, the vice-presidents and even the auditors. What has a board of directors to do but to clock in for their per diems and expenses? What, then, is it accountable for, and to whom?
As far as my colleagues on the Progressive Conservative task force on Crown corporations can determine, there is no clear chain of command either up or down. Any one of a half dozen interested Ministers can get in on the act and give their orders, but when it comes to carrying the can, what do we hear? Cabinet is collectively responsible; it was a decision of Cabinet.
Even that we could live with if we could believe it, but how can we when half the leadership candidates, Cabinet members, daily undermine that collective responsibility with impunity? The Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) and the Minister for Economic Development all question openly and publicly the policies they are responsible for and yet cling so tenaciously to office. One or the other. There is no honourable or honest middle ground.
Of course, it may be that it is we on this side of the House who are wrong. Perhaps we should not complain about the inefficiency and mismanagement of de Havilland and Cana-dair. Perhaps we should not worry about all the political appointees to these six-figure plums. Perhaps we should be
May 7, 1984

unconcerned about the secrecy, the Orders in Council which pervade the Crown corporations, the post-midnight manipulations such as that performed very early last Wednesday morning when at the stroke of a pen the sports pool became a lottery.
Perhaps we simply should not concern ourselves that the Parliament of Canada is now, and under C-24 will remain, powerless to demand an accounting of either Crown corporations or their nominally responsible Ministers. After all, Crown corporations now employ 263,000 people, 25,000 more than the Government of Canada. Last year they lost $4 billion. The Government of Canada lost $25 billion. That is small solace to the taxpayers who must underwrite such losses, the people who are owed accountability by all of us in public life, not just at election time but every day that we sit as Members of this House.
That above all else is the principle that Bill C-24 ignores. That more than anything is what is missing from this legislation-the obligation to see that these Crown corporations answer to their stockholders to no less of a degree than would the board and administration of any publicly-held and traded corporation or business enterprise.
These Crown corporations-Canadair, Canada Post, the CBC, Air Canada, Petro-Canada-do not exist in a vacuum. They are the very real property of the people of Canada, from the desk Knowlton Nash sits behind to the corner gas station with the Petro-Canada logo. If Members opposite forget, they should be reminded that it was their policy to have the latter, Petro-Canada, spend millions to convince us with their slogan "Petro-Canada, it's ours". Yes, it is ours, for better or for worse. The Crown corporations of Canada belong to the people of Canada. They are their property. The Government is only the steward of those investments, with no less responsibility to give a full and accurate accounting than any executor or trustee of an estate required to pass the accounts before the court each year.
That is the accountability which is required, that and nothing less. We, the 282 Members of this House, not only represent the people of Canada; we represent and hold the trust of the people of Canada. The court before which the accounts of Crown corporations, of government in all its form, must pass is this Parliament. We have not only the right but the duty to demand a full and complete report, not this pitiful sham called C-24. Nothing less can or will do.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to Bill C-24 today. The expanse of the proposed legislation is such that one could speak under the old rules for 40 minutes over and over again. It is quite restrictive to speak for only ten minutes. I will restrict myself to that.
I begin by saying that I am not opposed to Crown corporations. I do not think anyone on this side is opposed to Crown corporations when they are utilized to the extent and the need where private enterprise cannot provide the service. I am
Financial Administration Act
opposed to Crown corporations that abuse the public system and abuse the taxpayers' funds.
The purpose of this Bill is to amend the Financial Administration Act to provide greater Cabinet control over Crown corporations and greater accountability to Parliament. The statement of that purpose is one which I would have liked to have written myself because I feel that it is indeed the purpose of this Bill. The only question I have is whether or not the Bill follows up on that purpose.
Perhaps I may quote the words of Mr. J. Robert S. Prichard, a Professor of Law at Harvard Law School, who on November 29 to December 1, 1983, made a representation to the Conference on "The Board of Directors: Coping with Changing Expectations" sponsore by the Conference Board of Canada in Toronto. I am sure that government Members listened to and received copies of his comments. At that time, he said:
My concern is that the accountability mechanisms are failing us with the result that the viability of the Crown Corporation as a policy interest is being threatened.
He went on further to say:
-in attempting to respond to demands for increased accountability, the government has resorted to a complex web of multiple bureaucratic approvals, attempting to make Crown Corporations accountable to everyone in sight-Parliament, Treasury Board, Finance, Ministers, committees, officials, etc. In the course of making Crown Corporations nominally accountable to so many, they are in fact truly accountable to no one.
His comments caused me great concern, Mr. Speaker. He went on to make some recommendations to which I would have hoped the Government had paid attention. The first of those recommendations reads as follows:
First, reduce the problem to a manageable size: ... reduce the number of Crown Corporations that need to be kept accountable.
He went on to recommend the following:
Second, encourage-indeed mandate-processes that will clarify objectives for Crown Corporations: Without objectives we cannot derive performance standards. And without performance standards we cannot achieve accountability-
Later on in his speech, he recommended the following:
Third, follow Lord Macaulay's dictum: "Choose Wisely and Confide Liberally": That is, we should try to ensure that appointments to the Boards of Directors are of the highest quality-
The Government did not listen to that recommendation.
-and then, having chosen the directors wisely, we should confide liberally in the Board, giving it both the responsibility and the necessary power to do its job.
Another recommendation reads as follows:
Fourth, emphasize regular, reliable and timely reporting and disclosure policies: The current haphazard situation is utterly unacceptable and the case history of Canadair provides compelling evidence of the inadequacies of the current legislation.
He went on to make the following two recommendations:
Fifth, to the extent possible, minimize the bureaucratization of the interrelationship of Crown Corporations and the government-
Sixth, resist the temptation to achieve accountability through relying primarily on after-the-fact audits,-

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
Professor Prichard's final comment that day was the following:
Whether or not we move in that direction has now become a question of political will. And whether or not our government possesses that will is a judgment on which 1 can make no special claim to competence.
Has the Government addressed that problem, Mr. Speaker? Has it exhibited the will to which Professor Prichard refers? The legislation before us applies directly to about 183 Crown corporations and subsidiaries wholly owned by the federal Government. Parent Crown corporations are held accountable for all of their subsidiaries, investments and mixed enterprises. Definitions of relevant terms are substantially clarified. That is a general over-view of the Act.
Looking at this Bill in the light of accountability and fairness, I do not think that we could even stretch a curve in order to give this Bill a passing grade. The Bill provides the Governor in Council too much regulation-making power. We must bring more of the mechanics of regulations to the Bill. The Ministers have responsibility but no power under Bill C-24. Power over the appointment of directors and the approval of plans and budgets still resides with Cabinet.
Bill C-24 provides for an insufficient role for boards of directors to play. More power should be given to the boards of directors, particularly in the appointment of CEOs and auditors and the setting up of by-laws. We should create an onus of responsibility on the boards of directors.
Above all, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-24 provides for an insufficient role for Parliament to play. It states that all new parent Crown corporations will be formed only by special Act. However, it provides for no control over subsidiaries of parent Crown corporations. That is our greatest problem at the present time. As well, many existing Acts will allow for the establishment of Crown corporations of the parent type.
The clause in the Bill dealing with special investigations and comprehensive auditing is totally confusing. What is a special investigation? Who dictates what special investigations will take place? Who carries out those special investigations? Who reports them and to whom? Who finalizes them before they are reported to the House, Mr. Speaker?
Dealing with directives, Bill C-27 provided for compensation. Bill C-24 provides for none. Mention of the FBDB, the EDC and the Farm Credit Corporation should be added to Clause 99(7) of the Bill. Our interpretation of the Act is that it is not binding on the Crown.
After reading the clauses which refer to annual reports and trying to understand what is meant by them, one finds that the Treasury Board will still control the form and content of all annual reports of Crown corporations. That is the accountability which is contained in the Bill, Mr. Speaker. Accountability is still spread all over the place and is still not given to Parliament. No Minister of the Crown can be truly held accountable for the Crown corporations for which he is responsible.
I return to the final comment made by Professor Prichard and 1 will read it again, Mr. Speaker, as follows:
Whether or not we move in that direction has now become a question of political will. And whether or not our government possesses that will is a judgment on which I can make no special claim to competence.
I wish Professor Prichard were here to read this Act and to see the lack of political will displayed by the Government.
I would like to carry on, Mr. Speaker, but I see that my time is running short. If I had more time, I would discuss the issue of fairness as it relates to this Act and to Crown corporations. I do not believe we see Canada Post exhibiting fairness when it is entering the field of Consumers Distributing and competing with private enterprises and small corner hardware stores. What about the fairness of a Crown corporation like Air Canada and the fairness of the way the Government is treating employees of Nordair and people who wish to purchase shares in Nordair? I do not think that we see any fairness there, Mr. Speaker.
I could mention many aspects of this Bill and try to relate the accountability contained within the Bill to the issue of fairness to people in private enterprise and to Members of the House. There is no fairness in the Bill, Mr. Speaker, so I ask the Government to reconsider the Bill and to reconsider the need for accountability of Crown corporations before it imposes this on the people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join my colleagues in putting forward my concerns about the Bill which is now before the House. I do so because it creates the sense that it satisfies one of the legitimate concerns of Parliament, that is, the accountability of Crown corporations to Parliament. I do not believe that the Bill achieves that very noble and necessary objective. Certainly it will have the effect of making Crown corporations more the instruments or the creatures of the Government. I do not suggest that that is a bad thing. It is a good thing. Having had some limited experience in that regard, I believe that the Government should have more direct day-to-day control over the running of Crown corporations. That is the function of government. But I suggest that it is the function of Parliament to hold the Government and agencies of the Government accountable for the day-to-day spending activities of the Government, of Crown corporations and of agencies. Parliament has the responsibility of holding the Government and its agencies accountable for the money that we vote for them every year. I do not believe that this Bill satisfies that basic objective.
I remember the special committee on parliamentary reform, the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure, which made ten reports to this House. One of the reports dealt exclusively with the question of accountability. One of the recommendations in that report called for the establishement of a standing committee of the House to deal with Crown corporations. It called for a special standing committee of the House which would have the power to deal exclusively with Crown corporations, their day-to-day activities and how they conducted themselves in terms of the mandates that they were given by Parliament. Unfortunately, that report remains on
May 7, 1984

the Table of the House. It has not been dealt with by Parliament. Like so many of the other excellent recommendations of that committee, we have chosen to set it aside and relegate the responsibility to some future Parliament. I would say that that is a great pity.
I suspect that the genesis of this Bill stems not only from the growth in the number of Crown corporations, their size and financial strength, but also from the comments made by the Auditor General in his annual report of 1983. I would like to quote from paragraph 1.61 of that report. It reads:
The sheer size of the Crown-owned corporations makes the matter of accountability important. Crown-owned corporations employ over a quarter of a million people. With revenues of $40 billion in the fiscal year ended 31 March 1983 (up from $31.9 billion in the previous year) and expenses of $44.2 billion ($33.7 billion in the previous year). Crown-owned corporations form a huge segment of Canada's total affairs. Their very massiveness demands a proper accountability framework.
Nothing could be more clear, nothing could be more precise, than what the Auditor General said to us in that report. He went on to say, in paragraph 1.63:
In my view, it is a situation which must not be permitted to continue. While it does continue, parliamentarians are losing part of their fundamental right to be the representatives of their constituents in the crucial decisions of how tax dollars are to be deployed and accounted for.
Parliament-not the Government, but Parliament-was the concern being underlined by the Auditor General, the ability of Parliament to exercise its ancient and very important function of holding the Government accountable for how it spends taxpayers' dollars.
Other Members of the House in speaking on this Bill have made reference to the sheer size of Crown corporations, to the growth in the number of Crown corporations-and I underline this because it is important to emphasize it-and the growth in the number of subsidiaries and agencies of Crown corporations. I emphasize that because this Bill will not exercise any degree of statutory control in terms of accountability over subsidiaries of Crown corporations. Again I refer to the Auditor General's report of March 31, 1983, from which I found out that there were 72 parent corporations in Canada. Those 72 parent corporations controlled 114 subsidiary corporations. There were also 106 corporate investment subsidiaries, for a total of 292. As has already been outlined by my hon. colleague from Leeds-Grenville (Mrs. Cossitt), Crown corporations directly employ more people than the Government of Canada. According to the Auditor General, they employ a total of 263,000 people. The 72 parent corporations, at the end of fiscal year 1983, had assets of $71.7 billion. What is even more important is that they had total liabilities-here again I refer to the 72 parent corporations-in fiscal year 1983, of $64.3 billion. Clearly, it is a situation which is out of control.
What concerns me-and I go back to my opening comments-is that the Bill creates the perception that the Government somehow is addressing the concern expressed by the Auditor General, which has been expressed in many other public forums and also in this House, that not only has Parliament lost control over Government spending but that
Financial Administration Act
Parliament has no control whatsoever over Crown corporations and their subsidiaries.
The danger of involving oneself in this kind of rhetoric is that one could get carried away and say that all Crown corporations should be done away with. I, for one, would be the last to put that position forward. Crown corporations are a unique part of the Canadian way. If they are a unique and important part of the Canadian way, then somehow they have to be made accountable to Parliament. I would like to suggest ways in which that could be made possible. For example, why not have Crown corporations report directly to Parliament instead of to the Government? After all, we as Members of Parliament represent the shareholders of Crown corporations-the taxpayers of Canada. Why should they go to the Government first? They should come to the shareholders in terms of being represented by the Members of this House. That is number one. The second suggestion is: why should the Government not move now? It does not have to wait for the recommendations and bring in the entire report of the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedure. It could bring a measure now, through the good offices of the Government House Leader, and establish a standing committee of the House to deal with Crown corporations. In that way, Parliament would have a vehicle by which to exercise some degree of control over Crown corporations.
Indeed, I would suggest that these two very simple suggestions would go a considerable way in strengthening the Bill to allay the fears of people and in ensuring that this Bill addresses the concerns of the Auditor General and Parliament, and that we will somehow take control of Crown corporations.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss briefly some of the matters in this Bill relating to Crown corporations. The proposal before us would allow an amendment to the Financial Administration Act and, in essence, would give Cabinet greater control over what are sometimes referred to as Crown corporations. To a certain degree it would give greater accountability to Parliament but, through a number of loopholes or ways in which the Bill could get around the basic premise-and there are a number of them Parliament and the Members of the House of Commons and the Canadian people would not be made aware of what is going on in Crown corporations.
There are, according to some estimates, 183 or 186 Crown corporations of which the federal Government has 100 per cent ownership. The Government also has interest in about 315

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
other listed corporations, some of which are mixed enterprises, some are subsidiaries and some are associated with the subsidiaries or other types of ventures. There are 55 associated corporations which are less than 50 per cent owned by the Federal Government. It has 17 point mixed enterprises. It has 23 other corporate entities, which are not explained. It has 148 subsidiary corporations, and there are 72 parent Crown corporations. That makes a total of 315 listed Crown corporations. There are, however, disputes over certain other corporations as to which no one seems to know whether they are, in fact, Crown corporations.
The unfortunate thing about this Bill, Mr. Speaker, is that it provides so many loopholes and so many exceptions and the federal Government and the Cabinet can interfere so much. A number of Crown corporations, such as the Bank of Canada, the Canadian Wheat Board and the international development research centre, are going to be exempt from this entire structure set up under the Financial Administration Act. However, that is for now. Others can be exempted later by statute.
As all of us are aware, in the last few clauses of almost any statute or Bill that has been passed there are a few clauses which deal with regulations such as, "The Governor in Council can make regulations pertaining to ..." I am sure many times in the future regulations will sneak in to exempt such and such a corporation from the Financial Administration Act. It is done all the time and we are only too aware of it. I feel it would be better, frankly, for Cabinet, as the shareholder, to vote its shares at the annual meeting, to elect the directors and then leave it up to the directors to run the company, unless there is something of massive importance to the Canadian nation and to society for which it must give direction. I do not believe the Government should be involved in the day-to-day running, decision-making and reviewing of by-laws of each of the parent corporations and 114 subsidiaries.
Under this proposal the Cabinet makes the major strategic decisions. Parliament merely approves the creation, and if it comes around to it, the disposal of a Crown corporation. Budgets, although they may be put before Parliament, are always put together in such a flimsy form and with such lack of detail because of alleged commercial confidentiality, that it really must be considered a bit of a laugh.
The unfortunate thing today is that although most of the major corporations in this country and in other countries really try to select the appropriate directors and go to great pains and effort to try to get the right mix of directors so they can give the right direction as need be to the management, the only prerequisite in a Crown corporation is that a person have connection to the governing Party, which in this case is the Liberal Party which has been in power for so many years. Therefore, we see intelligent people such as Pierre Goyer, who, however, was a bit of a disaster as a Minister in this House, being appointed a director of Canadair where there is another disaster taking place. It would seem to me that a person should have proven himself in the corporate commercial world before being appointed director of a Crown corporation. However,
such is not the case. It has become a patronage tool. Cabinet has taken away most of the issues which directors should be discussing and has left the directors with certain criteria and guidelines which may be inappropriate. Cabinet has taken away the powers of the directors to direct and it has asked the directors to develop and implement the corporate plans, which I really believe is a management prerogative, and if management does not carry it out then the director should have the right to change the management.
Of course, under the terms of this legislation, Cabinet chooses the management, not the directors. Therefore, the directors are really toothless tigers, which is an unfortunate situation. For example, directors should appoint the auditors, whether it is Touche Ross Limited, Thorne Riddell Inc., Price Waterhouse Associates or whatever accounting firm is competent and capable. That is a normal every day obligation of the directors, a decision which is usually approved at annual meetings. But in this case they must consult the Minister or the Cabinet, which is just another way of allowing the Cabinet or the Ministers to interfere and to porkbarrel, making sure that their Liberal friends-as has been the case for so many years-are in there to mess around with the Crown corporation.
The Bill says they are to consult with the Ministers and Cabinet in other management affairs. Again, that is not what shareholders are allowed to do. As a shareholder in any one of our Canadian companies, one cannot go in and involve oneself in management affairs on a daily basis. All that shareholders can do is to wait until the next annual meeting or special meeting and vote, and by the pressure of their vote make their concerns known to the directors, who will, in turn, pass them on to management. Management would be unwise to ignore the interests of the shareholders, and I think any intelligent management would take cognizance of the fact that they have certain views. However, under this legislation, Cabinet has a right to meddle on a daily basis with the management affairs, and I feel that is wrong.
Cabinet can give directives, which are to be tabled within 15 days in Parliament unless the appropriate Minister feels that this would be detrimental to the commercial interests of a Crown corporation. We have heard, Mr. Speaker, the excuse that this is detrimental to the commercial viability of so many things, whether it be a FIRA application or a person applying for a grant under the RDIA program, formerly the DREE program. Unless you had a copy of their application in front of you, even though they were constituents, you would not be allowed to discuss it because, we are told, security is needed to protect the commercial nature of the project. Right there we have an exemption which, although directives can be given and Parliament is supposed to hear about them within 15 sitting days, is allowed just on the whim of a Minister.
There are many other areas I would like to speak about, Mr. Speaker, but unfortunately I see my time is running out. All I want to say is that I know our Party was so concerned at the proliferation of Crown corporations and the bad administration involved, it set up a task force, which has set forth a very
May 7, 1984

good report. I think the Government would have been wise to have read the report of that task force before it undertook the appointment of more Liberal appointees in the system.

Mr. Speaker, it is embarrassing to confess that with respect to Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act, I find myself not only confused but bewildered. I know some of my colleagues might allege that this is a permanent state of affairs for me, but I frankly do not understand what went on in the developmental process leading to Bill C-24. I am the first to acknowledge that we are in what is likely to be the last or penultimate session of this Parliament, what we normally call our pre-election session, when Government has historically been cautious in its legislation, bringing forward only that which it thinks is in its own best political interests. That is understandable. I sometimes deplore it but I think we have been living with that for well

over 100 years and none of us should be too surprised at it. But what confuses me is that I did not think, and I still do not, that there was any political downside to an Act dealing rather substantively with Crown corporations. I do not see where the political risk is. In fact, I think it is a good political issue no matter what side of the House you are sitting on.
In my view, Bill C-24 could have been a very substantive, tough and realistic piece of legislation without any political risk whatsoever. I do not want to be harsh, but I think we are dealing with a cosmetic Bill, one that might be termed, were it dealing with some other subject matter, a political Bill in the last session of the House before an election.
The Government has certainly had lots of time. I can recall that when I first came here 12 years ago, the Government commenced the study of Crown corporation control and accountability. More than seven years ago, this Government promised legislation to reform Crown corporation control and accountability. If, Sir, this is the result of over a decade of Government study, then frankly, to be as charitable as I can, it is extraordinarily disappointing.
There is a multitude of flaws in this Bill. One could take almost any one of a dozen aspects, but time is limited and I want to deal with something that others in the House have dealt with. Because I find it so incredible, I think the point needs reinforcing, that is, Mr. Speaker, the role and responsibility of the board of directors of Canadian Crown corporations. I admit that a Crown corporation has certain unique elements, but if it is engaged in commercial or quasi-commercial activity, then surely it must bear some resemblance to a corporation undertaking the same thing in the private sector. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson), in opening the debate for our Party said that: "In effect, Bill C-24 would convert board of directors into advisory boards with little or no power". I absolutely agree. If I had any quarrel with that, it would be that the Hon. Member was being a little too charitable to the Government. I am not sure that these boards of directors should really be called in the truest sense advisory boards whose advice would, as a rule of thumb, be given some credibility even if it were not followed. Frankly, an advisory board gains its reputation by its clout, power or prestige, of which obviously there is none in these Crown corporations as proposed by Bill C-24. Frankly, Sir, I cannot see anything very prestigious about the proposed boards of directors of Canadian Crown corporations. The greatest flaw is the inability of a board, Mr. Speaker, to choose the chief executive officer, establishing the tenure and supervise him or her. I have always believed that to be a hallmark of any board of directors. However, in this legislation Cabinet, not the board, appoints the chief executive officer. Cabinet establishes tenure. Cabinet sets the remuneration. With respect to some Crown corporations, Cabinet not only appoints the CEO, it appoints others at the executive level. Also, the election of a chairman of the board is not made by the board from among its members. Cabinet appoints the chairman. Cabinet appoints the auditors as well. Cabinet establishes the dividend policy of the corporation.

I suppose the question is, Mr. Speaker: Why the flaws? Again, trying to be as charitable as I can, I presume no one directed his or her mind to the principle of responsibility when the legislation was drafted. If one had started with the Minister responsible for a particular Crown corporation, then I think there would have been a natural flow. The Minister has to be put in the position, if he is to exercise his judgment with any degree of responsibility, of being able to say, "I am responsible, my job is on the line, and I am going to go out and get the very best board of directors I can find". He is not going to give them seven, eight and nine year terms. If they do not measure up to the standard which the Minister needs to protect him or her as a Minister and to discharge his or her responsibility, they should go. That to me would seem to be the logical flow, Mr. Speaker. At that point the board is going to say, "We had better get the best chief executive officer we can find in this whole country to run this Crown corporation. Unless we do, we, the board of directors, are going to be gone". If that had been the starting point, Mr. Speaker, we would never have got into this mess.
As I say, it is inconceivable that there is a downside. I do not understand why any Cabinet Minister would want to proceed in that direction. Obviously there are political appointments and everyone has his input on the Government side, particularly Cabinet Ministers. But when your job is on the line, I would think it not only behooves you, but it is, in the most crass way, in the self-interest of a Cabinet Minister to get the very best board he or she can get his or her hands on and say to them: "You are running this company, so find a chief executive officer and other executives who will make sure that you and I look good". Obviously that was not the starting point. I do not know what was. I do not know whether this was a bureaucratic Bill that no one thought through in a business or political sense. I do not believe the Government has done a good political job here.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling that I have one minute left. The analogy to a commercial corporation is not perfect. I understand that. There are no shareholders in the sense in which we know them. One could say that every taxpayer is a shareholder. I do not think that destroys the natural analogy to a company in the private sector. If I were the Minister, I would say that I am the trustee for every shareholder and that every taxpayer is a shareholder. As a trustee I would be very careful because a trustee's responsibilities are even greater than those of a Cabinet Minister.
I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are signalling for me to conclude. I would like to go on for another hour, Mr. Speaker. However, I am not going to ask for unanimous consent to do that. I thank you for your patience. I deeply regret that this Bill, which I thought was very very important, has turned out to be such a disappointment for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have a few minutes to speak on the Bill before us this afternoon. This Bill could be a very important development in
the life of Crown corporations in this country. Unfortunately, the way it has been put before the House of Commons, it will certainly not be anywhere near adequate. I do not think it will come as a surprise to Members of the House that we in this corner of the House have a very positive position with regard to Crown corporations. We recognize that they are a very important part of Canadian life. We recognize that many years ago governments in our country realized that with Canada's great geographical area and small population there were many services that the private sector either could not or would not provide. Therefore, it became incumbent upon the governments to put forward this bill having to do with Crown corporations.
Since that time the Canadian economy has evolved into what we refer to in this country as a mixed economy, with a large private sector and a substantial public sector in the form of Crown corporations and other government bodies under Crown control or partly owned by Crown corporations. Unfortunately, in recent years the credibility of Crown corporations has been called into question. I believe we can lay a lot of the blame for that on the Government. It has not kept an adequate control on the Crown corporations.
What has been the purpose of some of these Crown corporations, Mr. Speaker? In some cases, such as that of PetroCan, they have provided a commercial entry into an area of the economy. In other cases, their purpose has been to develop a certain part of the country. In many instances, they provide a service. One example is provincial telephone companies, which in much of Canada are Crown corporations. I believe that electric companies in the entire country are Crown corporations. In some parts of Canada, automobile insurance has been taken over by Crown corporations with great success. There are a lot of very good success stories about Crown corporations. I would say that most of them in the country have been successes.
When my friend, the Hon. Member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller), was speaking earlier this afternoon, he made reference to the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. I am very familiar with that Crown corporation, Mr. Speaker, since a large part of its business is done in my constituency. I would like to relate its experience very briefly.
This corporation moved into an industry which was in terrible shape in the late 1960s. At that time it was controlled by a number of private corporations, which were not acting at all in the best interests of the fishermen, the people for whom the industry should be providing the most benefit. These private corporations were operating in a dog-eat-dog fashion. They basically controlled the Fishermen through their initial payments and, in most cases, lack of a final payment, and through the provision of start-up fees for getting into the business at the beginning of each season. In many ways they were endangered employees. Most of them were fairly poor as a result of that.
In the late 1960s, provincial Governments asked the federal Government to step in and fix it up. The federal Government moved in and provided a very successful corporation. At the

present time, fishermen in most of western Canada who come under that body are able to earn at least an adequate living, if not a great living. I certainly do not want to give the impression that this is a perfect corporation. It is not. There are many improvements which could be made. However, there is no arguing with the fact that the situation for the workers is vastly better than it was previously.
What happens to so many corporations? In recent months we have heard much about the computer company which lost hundreds of millions of dollars. We have certainly heard of the scandalous situation of Canadair and de Havilland. We all know the story of Canada Post. I am most amused by the quarterly reports which we receive from the Chief Executive Officer of Canada Post, Mr. Warren, informing us how much things have improved since he took over the corporation. Almost ironically, within days of receiving a quarterly report I often receive a letter from a constituent telling me a horror story he or she has experienced in getting mail delivered.
What should we do, Mr. Speaker? In his opening comments last week my friend, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo), said that we must give these corporations a clear mandate with public responsibility and public direction. We then must ensure that they stick to that mandate and operate within the objectives which this House gives them when the corporation is established. That does not mean that we are going to interfere in the day-to-day operations. Indeed, if this piece of legislation is to give the Cabinet the right to interfere in the day-to-day operations of Crown corporations, then I think the Bill has to be changed. The responsibility for day-today operations must be left up to the board of directors and the chief executive officer. However, we must ensure that Crown corporations, like any other corporation, operate with sound management in the best interests of the shareholders, who are the taxpayers of the country.
I would like to make a few comments on the parliamentary reform committee that the Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) was talking about a few moments ago. You well know what I am speaking of, Mr. Speaker. You were one of the leading members of that committee. You are aware that we debated at some length the need for controls and government accountability in many different areas, including Crown corporations and Departments. We received some degree of accountability through the fact that government Departments must now submit their reports to standing committees. However, we also identified the fact that there are many corporations which do not put out annual reports. There are many corporations which are partially owned by the federal Government that should be accountable to the Parliament of this country.
As the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) pointed out, we called for the establishment of a committee to which all Crown corporations, quasi-Crown corporations and partly owned corporations will report. As the Hon. Member said, it is lamentable that this report still lies on the Table of

the House and that nothing has been done about it. It calls the good faith of the Government into question and begs the question as to whether the Government has something to hide about the operation of these Crown corporations. We would certainly hope that is not so, but when we see the scandals of recent weeks, notably that of Canadair and de Havilland, after their huge losses, having had the nerve to grant bonuses to some of their senior executives, we think it is time that Members of the House of Commons, who are the representatives of the shareholders, have a say in how those corporations are run.
In closing, I think that most Members would agree, and certainly we in this Party believe, that Crown corporations are too important to the well-being of this country to be left alone. It is very important that they maintain their credibility. For that reason we believe that through this piece of legislation and amendments to it, through the adoption of the recommendation made by the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedures for a standing committee, Crown corporations will be made accountable to the Parliament of Canada.
