speechtext:
If they remained silent, they might learn something, but that would be asking a great deal. The Government has been studying Crown corporations since 1972 and has been promising reforms since 1977. We have read the various reports of the Auditor General and of the Public Accounts Committee. We have had the Lambert Commission and various reports by academics. There is a consensus that something must be done in Canada to bring Crown corporations under control. However, Bill C-24 is totally inadequate. I do not know why the Government has bothered with it.
Bill C-24 entails a clear and major erosion of Parliament's control over Crown corporations. Of course, there was not that much control to begin with. Parliament will have no control over the creation of subsidiaries by Crown corporations. A Minister need not get parliamentary approval for the creation of a Crown corporation if he or she already has the power to do so through an existing Act of Parliament. There are at least 12 pieces of legislation that give Ministers such power.
Bill C-24 gives immense regulatory power to the Government. Virtually every clause of the Bill contains a regulationmaking power by which the Government, in effect, defines how that clause will operate or which Corwn corporations will be exempted from the requirements imposed by that clause. In effect, the Bill states that regulations can change the clause, so the Government is offering nothing to the people of Canada

May 7, 1984
Financial Administration Act
except to ask then to trust it. That has been the problem with Crown corporations in the past.
There are few, if any, criteria in the Bill which constrain or establish a framework within which the Governor in Council may make regulations. Bill C-24 converts boards of directors into advisory boards with little or no real power. In the private sector, the principal role of the board of directors is to recruit the chief executive officer and to supervise his stewardship of the corporation. According to Bill C-24, the Cabinet appoints the chief executive officer and sets his tenure and remuneration. Cabinet also appoints the chairman and the auditor, and it approves the by-laws and may even make laws for the board of directors.
The basic problem is that the Crown corporations do not know to whom they are responsible. Real authority is not exercised by a Cabinet Minister but by Treasury Board, groups of Ministers or the Cabinet as a whole. It is certainly not exercised by an individual Minister. As a result of being accountable to so many ministers, Crown corporations are accountable to no one. However, I suggest that this is probably to the Government's advantage, because what Minister would want to be totally responsible to any Crown corporation after the mess that has been made of them over the years?
The proliferation of Crown corporations has meant that the task of ensuring their accountability has become much more difficult and really much more important. No matter how good a government's accountability regime, it will not work so long as the trend to the creation of more Crown corporations continues.
The first step under Bill C-24 should have been to reduce the number of Crown corporations that we need. Every means should be utilized, either by selling them, giving them away, winding them up or making them smaller. However, we certainly do not need the present number of Crown corporations.
The increase in Crown corporations has not been accompanied by a comprehensive overhaul of the legal and administrative machinery for ensuring their accountability. We have not heard the objectives of Crown corporations properly clarified. Boards of directors should be obliged to articulate their understanding of their corporations' objectives on a regular basis. If the Government does not agree with those objectives, it can exercise its power as the sole shareholder to direct a change.
It is not clear to me from this Bill to whom the Government wants the Crown corporations to be accountable. Is it Parliament, Treasury Board, Finance Ministers, standing committees or various government officials? They are nominally accountable to many but truly accountable to no one which, I suggest, is evident from the scandals of the last few years. There should be regular, reliable and timely reporting and disclosure policies for all Crown corporations. Why is that not set out clearly in the Bill? Appointments to boards should be of the highest quality, and the Government must have the will to forgo patronage. Directors' terms should be for one year, not multiple years, and performance, not presumption, should govern the appointment and reappointment.
Boards should be given responsibility and the necessary power to do the job. Furthermore, interrelationship with Government should be streamlined, simple, expeditious and effective. There should be no ambiguity in these objectives.
I think an analogy with the private sector is worth-while pointing out. The private sector involves shareholders. In the case of Crown corporations, the shareholders are the people of Canada, and through them, their elected representatives. I am a shareholder in every Crown corporation, but those Crown corporations do not give me the information that I would receive as a shareholder in a private company. The board of directors should select the chief executive officer, as it does in the private sector. While I admit that the Government can appoint the board of directors, the members of any board of directors should have some ability to operate those corporations.
Every Crown corporation should make a quarterly report as well as provide financial statements. Their financial accounting should be conducted in the same way as is done in any other company and they should not hide the truth from their shareholders, the people of Canada, as they do now.
The Canadair, de Havilland and other scandals have cost me as a taxpayer million of dollars. I find the attitude of this Government in this Bill C-24, which is its mirror image, does absolutely nothing to clean up the horrible mess it has created. It is shameful to bring this Bill before the House in this form. All I can say to this tired old Government is, for heaven's sake, in this case in the interest of all Canadians, why not withdraw this Bill, clean up the act and make Crown corporations accountable to the House of Commons? Let us get some facts out on a quarterly basis so that we can save a dollar now and then for the taxpayer, about which this Government does not seem to care. What's a billion? Canadair can tell you what a billion is. The taxpayers of Canada as voting shareholders will have a chance to tell you, Members opposite, in terms of your tenure as the board of directors of this country what they think. You, over there, have to be thrown out for the benefit of all.

Mr. Speaker,
I would like to say a few words. The Government opposite has a tendency to wait until the later months of spring as we get into the time of adjournment to bring in a whole host of complex and overdue pieces of legislation, such as Bill C-24, to create the illusion of progress and activity on behalf of the people whom they have poorly represented these past 14 years. That is what Bill C-24 is all about. It is the same in the case of Bill C-19, the omnibus Bill which purports to amend so many aspects of the Criminal Code including sentencing, computer crime, drinking drivers, fire arms, and a whole long list of important measures of reform. They have all been thrust upon this House in the dying moments of a dying Government merely to create the illusion of action. Here we are once again faced with a piece of legislation. Suddenly the Government awakened to the realization that the Crown corporations,
May 7, 1984

which it has created in abundance over the past 14 years, perhaps 15 years under the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), have been disastrous in their consequence to the people of Canada. It has not mattered whether these Crown Corporations have been in a form to regulate and their regulatory powers have run out of control. It has not mattered whether they were corporations created to fulfil some great and important national purpose by way of providing a monopoly service to the people of Canada, which then became deficit ridden and top heavy with bureaucracy. It does not matter whether we are talking about the Crown corporations that were created to generate a positive industrial climate by developing new initiatives in different areas in which Canada had not previously been engaged. In all of these cases the Government opposite has failed miserably to bring these Crown corporations under control, to make them accountable to the people, who, after all, ought to be considered as the shareholders. If the Crown is to operate corporations in the name of the people of Canada, what better place to make them accountable than in this House of Commons where those who represent the people of Canada are empowered and should be welcome to overview the management of such major enterprises? As other Members have pointed out we have now created, at last count I think, over 450 corporations of this sort in Canada. We cannot count all of the subsidiary little creatures that have spun off from the major corporations, because they are being created virtually day after day without the House of Commons and the Parliament of Canada being invited to scrutinize the rationale, the raison d'etre for the creation of these new agencies.
If we look at Bill C-24 in detail, we can see that it will not go too far to resolve this fundamental question of accountability. One of the reasons Crown corporations have not been held accountable is that the legislation under which they were created, where indeed that legislation has been debated in the House of Commons, is more or less just a shell, a framework in which broad powers of discretion are granted to the Governor in Council. If we look at the detail of this Bill, we see no means of bringing this lack of direction under control. In fact, the regulation making powers of the Governor in Council will be enhanced under the provisions of this Bill.
We have also pointed out that the boards of these corporations and their chairmen are not directly accountable to Parliament. Under existing legislation, most of the boards are accountable to responsible Ministers. But under the proposals contained in this Bill, Mr. Speaker, that level of responsibility-accountability to a specifically designated Minister- would be diminished and the corporations and their boards would be asked to report to a Cabinet committee, thus the direct responsibility to the House of Commons and to a responsible Minister would be diminished even further.
If we were to prepare a Bill of this nature dealing with the necessary structure and framework under which Crown corporations were required to operate, it would begin with the notion that no Crown corporation has the perpetual right to existence. We would begin with the notion that Crown corpo-
Financial Administration Act
rations would be required to come annually to Parliament to justify their financial plans and their borrowing requirements. Members of the board would be called before parliamentary committees to demonstrate their expertise in conducting the affairs of a corporation. When such a corporation was established under legislation to serve certain aspects of a national interest, that is to say to provide transportation in remote parts of the country, which was the original mandate for the CNR and Air Canada, then it would be incumbent upon the directors of that corporation to come before Parliament annually and point out the extent to which that national interest was being served.
The question in the case of Air Canada of meeting the convenience and the necessity of an affordable service to the travelling public, for example, would have to be addressed by the chairman of that corporation. He would be accountable to Parliament for the continuation of his responsibility, not accountable to the Cabinet or the Prime Minister.
The system of politically appointing the chief executive officer or the chairman of a Crown corporation and his board-I should correct that slightly, the chief executive officer is not supposed to be a political appointee, although in many cases he is, but it is quite evident that the chairmen or chair persons of major Crown corporations are appointed for political reasons-that practice must come to an end, Mr. Speaker. If a Crown corporation is to be accountable to the taxpayers of Canada in whose interests it is supposed to operate, then the Parliament of Canada-just as in a private corporation where the board of directors is selected by the votes of the shareholders-the Members of this House of Commons, should have the right to examine the proposed occupants of the key positions on the board of a corporation, and indeed in some case this House should vote on those positions.
Another area where Crown corporations should be brought under control is their almost unlimited ability to borrow money privately in the name of Her Majesty without adequate overview by the people's representatives here in the House of Commons. In other words, the extent to which Crown corporations incur financial responsibility must be strictly controlled. There ought to be a relationship drawn between the equity, the asset value of the Crown corporation, and the amount of liability it incurs. Those liabilities should be permanently entered on the books of that corporation as a liability to be cleared from the earnings of that corporation, unless the chairman and board of directors can justify the deficits from the point of view of fulfilling some element of the national need.
There is no provision in this legislation to restrict the ability of Crown corporations to spawn subsidiaries. There is no provision to prevent Government Ministers from creating Crown corporations merely as a smokescreen, to remove from their area of responsibility a corporation that is going wrong, as was the case with CDIC. The responsible Minister did not

want to have to account for the disastrous and tragic mismanagement of Canadair, de Havilland and Eldorado Nuclear. Therefore, the Government hived them off into a new subsidiary organization, CDIC, whose purpose to this date has not been clearly stated in this House of Commons. It appears to be a ruse to deny parliamentarians the right to scrutinize those corporations by removing them one step from the overview of this Parliament.
When we look at the track record, we see that Canada Post is incurring annually a deficit in excess of $500 million. We should look at the deficits incurred by the CBC. We can turn on the CTV television network and obtain virtually the same quality programs without incurring a deficit of half a billion dollars a year. We have to ask if this Bill is adequate.
In conclusion, it is obvious to the people of Canada that a major overhaul is essential in the management of our Crown corporations. This Bill will just not fill the bill.

Mr. Speaker, in joining with my colleagues in speaking to this Bill I wish to spend my allotted time on Bill C-24, an Act to amend the Financial Administration Act dealing with Crown corporations, by addressing one very crucial aspect of this legislation, one that is fundamental to my Party's view of financial accountability. It is important because, while it demonstrates a gaping flaw in Bill C-24, it is characteristic of the current Liberal's inclination to snub a tradition of trust with the electorate at the same time as it takes steps to legislate sloppiness and protect bunglers. This Bill legislates against the tradition of ministerial responsibility.
As the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) outlined in his speech opening second reading, this Bill once again ducks the whole notion of ministerial accountability. We have heard from political commentators that the so-called Trudeau era ushered in the practice of collegial decision-making. I suggest that Bill C-24 provides eloquent testimony to the failure that this practice has been in terms of public policy formulation and the efficient operation of the Government of Canada.
Collegiality might better be viewed as the attempt to protect the slender reputations of political appointees who found themselves stuck in ministerial roles demanding far more managerial moxie than they could ever muster. Except for geographical coincidence, they should never have been considered ready to manage anything more than their golf scores. Even then, they would have needed to have a foursome.
The Hon. Member for Calgary South outlined my Party's position on ministerial accountability. He said:
-we will never solve the problems of Crown corporations until Crown corporations come under an effective regime of individual ministerial responsibility. C-24 goes in the opposite direction. The individual minister is nothing but a post box. The real authority is exercised by Cabinet or the Treasury Board-groups of Ministers, rather than individual Ministers... In being accountable to so many Ministers, Crown corporations will continue to be accountable to no one.
The Government maintains that this Bill seeks to address the problems of the accountability of Crown corporations, as pointed out in various studies ranging from the Auditor General's report, the Lambert report, and its other self-appointed experts. This is nonsense. What this Bill does is to enshrine all the worst inclinations this Government has demonstrated in unnecessary bureaucratization of a process that clearly demands the hands-on intervention of responsible Ministers held accountable by Parliament. In Bill C-24 we are offered regulation instead of responsibility, mud instead of stone, and spinelessness instead of gumption.
Let me offer a case in point, one that illustrates the often useful vehicle of a Crown corporation which has gone sour, and worse. During 1966 and 1967, the federal Government was busying itself creating the National Museum's board. As originally envisaged, the board was to offer centralized services to the National Museums and Galleries. However, in settling on a model for this board, the Government chose the structure of the British Coal Board to oversee the best interest of Canadians in housing and exhibiting their heritage in an educational fashion. Think of the example of the British Coal Board. Needless to say, what Canadians actually got was a messy bureaucratic structure which takes up nearly three-quarters of all monies allocated in the federal budget to museums. That way we see the current administration able to hide away the National Museums Construction Board, which will not be audited until 1989, which is hell-bent on building new galleries and museums before the Minister, who should be responsible, has even begun to devise the programs by which they will be run.
The viability of the Crown corporation as a vehicle for public interest is being threatened by the tendency for Ministers to hide behind bureaucracy rather than to send clear signals to that bureaucracy and then be prepared to stand in Parliament and defend them. This Bill demonstrates no newfound desire to open Crown corporations to public scrutiny, to let the interest groups regularly and systematically react, whether it be through the vehicle of parliamentary committees or whatever. On the contrary, Bill C-24 has the seeds of even more blatant attempts by our collegial federal Cabinet to spend its way into the political hearts of Canadians while it eats its way into the future of their children and grandchildren.
There are many illustrations. When talking about responsibility, I think not only of the responsibility in cultural areas but of the responsibility in public transport. In the last few days I have been reviewing the service of VIA Rail into the Kitchener-Waterloo area. I spoke to passengers about that Crown corporation, the funding for which is still a $l-vote in the Estimates. It is a corporation which is impossible to influence even though the citizens are directly affected by it. I regularly found that the insensitivity of this Crown corporation is such that all of the advertisements in the Kitchener-Waterloo area relate to national travel and it is impossible for passengers wishing to travel from Kitchener-Waterloo to Toronto to find those trips advertised by a government agency in their own newspaper.

I could go on. My colleagues have been outlining the failure of this Bill to meet the reality of what we see as being a substructure of Government running amok. Each of us could spend hours illustrating this from our own experiences.
Let me conclude my remarks by indicating that not only is the lack of ministerial responsibility one of the fundamental shortfalls of the Bill but, as well, the scope of the Bill is very limited. Bill C-24 does not cover many of the major structural problems related to Crown corporations as a whole. It is, for example, silent on the matter of internal government organization and on the matter of privileges and immunities of Crown corporations. It is silent about whether we will find more Crown corporations hiding behind the Combines Investigation Act and whether public servants should serve on the boards of Crown corporations. It is silent about the extent of the Government of Canada's accounting entity and the creation of parliamentary oversights. In addition, the Bill covers only wholly-owned corporations. It does not apply to the more than 100 mixed and joint enterprises that exist.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest that the public is not being fooled by this cosmetic effort. Bill C-24 demonstrates that the Government is out of step with the thinking of Canadians and their desire for accountability of the tax dollars that are spent. I join with my colleagues in asking the Government to withdraw this Bill and return to Parliament with something which will really tackle the serious concerns which have been reflected in the House.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to participate in today's debate concerning the control and accountability of Crown corporations. Crown corporations have played a very long and valuable role in the development of Canada. As long ago as 1841, the joint Governments of Upper and Lower Canada, the Government of the United Provinces, set up a board of public works to build canals in the country which was known as Canada at that time. As long ago as 1906, Ontario Hydro was established as a Crown corporation which had a monopoly on producing electricity in the Province of Ontario. That corporation was set up by a Conservative Government in 1906.
Many provinces have found it useful and necessary to set up Crown corporations, most of which have been patterned after a monopoly, with regard to the offering of telephone services. As an example of that, I cite the Government of my own Province of Saskatchewan and the Government of the neighbouring Province of Manitoba. In terms of providing services for the new airline industry, for example, Trans-Canada Air Lines was established as a Crown corporation to provide service right across the country.
I suppose there are many different ways to look at Crown corporations, because there is a great range of work that can be done by Crown corporations and a great many ways in which Crown corporations may function. Some very useful and beneficial Crown corporations do exist. Corporations which are often thought of as Crown corporations, such as the
Financial Administration Act
Canadian Wheat Board, have been very useful. The Canadian Wheat Board does an excellent job of marketing farmers' grain in western Canada, the area for which it has responsibility, and it does so in the most efficient manner possible. Without extracting a profit from its users, it returns all of its benefits and all of its surplus funds back to the farmers who use the Wheat Board. When Crown corporations function in that way, they provide a benefit to the users and a benefit to the economy as a whole.
We have seen examples of Crown corporations being created to bail out investors who have done a poor job. We saw this happen in 1919 when the Borden Government established the Canadian National Railways by rolling three nearly bankrupt railway companies into one. The shareholders of those companies were protected because the Government took over the liabilities of those railways and kept on paying dividends by way of interest. The CNR had a great deal of difficulty functioning because what had happened was that the Government had in effect taken over the assets of those railways for far more than their market value.
A similar example occurred a few years earlier when the Liberal Government of Saskatchewan began to establish a government grain elevator corporation, the establishment of which was against its will. The farmers insisted on having a government-operated elevator company in order to avoid some of the practices in which the free enterprise elevator owners were engaged. The Government of the day did not want to enter into the elevator business but was forced into it, by the farmers. Consequently, the Government chose to buy all of the losing elevators across the country. It bought the poorest elevators in the poorest locations with the worst managers and combined them all. By golly, the Government was right. The Government could not run an elevator company. Since that time, many other corporations have been set up by the Crown that have not followed that route but have been very efficient and effective. It is simply a matter of what the mandate of a Crown corporation is and what the written and unwritten agendas of the management of the Crown corporations are.
I believe that a Bill which would attempt to make Crown corporations more accountable and would set out rules for them to follow would be of some use to the country. The effects of the proposed legislation have been indicated several times in the speeches we have heard up to this point. Given the few moments left to me, I would like to point out that we have some questions regarding the ability of this legislation to provide the necessary control and accountability, given the fact that there now exist Crown corporations which act as holding companies.
The proposed Canadian Development and Investment Corporation would act in effect like a little Argus or Power Corporation. There would be a great many other second, third and fourth-ranked Crown corporations under that corporation. Under this legislation, the Parliament of Canada would only be setting out accountability provisions for the granddaddy corporation, the CDIC, and would not have very much say or
3482

May 7, 1984
Capital Punishment
control over what goes on in the second, third and fourth-level corporations.
As well, another form of involvement of Crown corporations which we are seeing quite often is the entry of Crown corporations into joint ventures and the setting up of other Crown corporations in which the parent Crown corporation is a one-third or one-half shareholder. This legislation does not make clear at all how the Parliament of Canada will be able to control those assets, which are under the name of the Crown and managed by a Crown corporation but exist beyond the control of Members of Parliament and beyond the accounting process that is set up by this legislation. We do not think that those questions have been adequately answered at this point in time.
We believe that the legislation should take those kinds of real life, current-day problems into account when it goes to committee. We feel, therefore, that the legislation needs some further amendment and further strengthening if indeed parliamentarians will be able to make the Crown corporations of the country accountable to them on behalf of the people of Canada who act as the shareholders of these corporations.

that Bill C-214, an Act to amend the Criminal Code (death sentences), be now read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I hope it is the intention of the House to pass this measure, because the people of Canada are getting tired of waiting for the reinstatement of capital punishment.
I want to deal with the problem today from the viewpoint of the man on the street, and from the viewpoint of 85 per cent of the people who sent me here. First, I think the terms should be defined. In the Bill, capital punishment means the death
penalty for the murder of another human being that is deliberately planned and executed, and where the person committing the act is found guilty beyond the shadow of a doubt. I want to make it clear that if there is any doubt whatsoever, the execution should not take place, in order to do away with the suggestion that we may hang the wrong man.
The first point I would like to deal with is that it is time the long moratorium on capital punishment ended. The people want it to end, and I think statistics will show that it should end. Canadians are angry. They believe in democracy and they want to know why the Government of Canada is not reflecting their wishes.
What are their wishes? According to the polls, the vast majority of people want the death sentence reinstated for first degree murder, where there is no shadow of a doubt. In 1972, the polls showed that 63 per cent of the people wanted the death penalty reinstated. In 1975, it rose to 69 per cent, and 79 per cent if it involved the death of a police officer. In 1983, the polls showed that 85 per cent of the people wanted capital punishment reinstated. When 85 per cent of the people of the country want something done, surely it is the responsibility of the government in power to reflect that thinking in the legislation. That many people cannot be wrong.
We live in a democracy. I do not accept the theory that the Government is providing leadership. His the people whom we are representing. When I knocked at doors in my own riding, more than 85 per cent of the people wanted capital punishment reinstated. If I did not stand for that, I would have had to tell them so, and I am doubtful if they would have elected me.
Why is the Canadian public feeling terrorized? Why are women afraid to walk in the streets of our cities after dark and sometimes before dark? Why is it not safe to put your can in an underground parking lot, or even in a parking lot above the ground in some cases? I think there are a number of reasons. There are too many murderers walking the streets. We do not know when those who are in prison are going to get out.
There was a very definite example of that just in the last day or so with a man who strangled four women. One of them was a schoolteacher in Calgary; the other three women, I believe, were from Quebec. He strangled them. A sex maniac. What happened? He was supposed to get a life sentence, but he was out at a fancy restaurant for dinner without enough guards to look after him. He went to the washroom and he escaped. He could have killed another woman. Fortunately, he was caught before he did that. It is not good enough for the Minister to say, as he did this afternoon, "I am not sure what went wrong". I know what went wrong. The man should have been executed after he murdered the first or second person. We should not have waited until he murdered four people.
How many times does this happen in Canada with murderers committing their second, third and fourth murder? The bleeding hearts of the country say, "We are rehabilitating them". I would have laughed, if it were not so sad, when the Hon. Minister said today that the chap took sexual therapy. Well, sexual therapy did not do Boden much good. I am
May 7, 1984

doubtful if it is doing anyone else much good. What is wrong is that we are catering to our murderers. We are giving more attention to the murderers than we are to the victims. The people of Canada are getting fed up with it.
Another case-and I do not want to deal with this in detail because I would like to deal with it at another time-is that of Clifford Robert Olson. He murdered 11 young people, people who were in the spring of their lives. He deliberately planned and murdered those young people. What he did to them before he murdered them God only knows. I do not say that in a profane way. Of course, Olson knows the abuse to which he may have submitted those young people before he murdered them and before he buried them. Then he bragged that he killed at lot more than 11 people. He tells us that he killed several more in the United States. Now he wants to write a book and make money from the deaths of the kids. It has gone too far and the people are getting fed up with this bleeding heart business.
Let us look at Brown and Peters in my own riding. They went out and searched to find a woman or girl whom they could sexually abuse, mutilate and then cover with gasoline and burn the evidence. One young married woman who ran out of gas happened to be their victim. It could could have been your daughter or your wife, Mr. Speaker, who happened to be on that road that night. But it was a young lady. If that was not enough, a short time afterward they watched stores to see if they could find a young girl who was left alone. Finally they found a store, went in the back way and took her out. They mutilated, abused her, and then covered her with gasoline and burned her. What happened to them? They got life. I would not be surprised if they are out on parole right now. There are so many bleeding hearts in this country who think that such men can be rehabilitated, men who are deliberately committing murder, who get their kicks out of murder. The kick they should get is at the end of a rope, and it should be their last kick.
There is also the Shearing case in British Columbia, that of a man who murdered three generations all in one night. He killed them, burned them and tried to destroy the evidence. It was carefully planned. He did not know the two families. It might have been you and your wife in the trailer, Mr. Speaker, but it happened to be those two particular families. Who knows what other murderers are lurking beside some national park waiting for the same thing to happen? In the way these murderers are treated afterward, there is certainly no deterrent. They are put in prison and they are given special attention. They are guarded from other prisoners. The other prisoners would not stand for it. There would be another murder if Olson was ever let loose in a prison. But do not worry, he will get out. "Life" does not mean a life sentence any more. Life means 20 years or 25 years, if it means that much. The prisoner is then supposedly rehabilitated. Yes, just like Boden. We are fortunate that Boden did not commit another murder. No wonder the Canadian people are terrorized. "Life" does not mean life. If it did, perhaps 85 per cent of the people of this country would not want capital punish-
Capital Punishment
rrient returned. "Life" does not mean life; it means 15 years or 20 years, and less than that in some cases.
Shearing got 25 years, and what did the judge say? I quote from part of his comments when sentencing, " . .. this senseless, brutal, cold blooded murder of six innocent people, three generations, murdered". For what? So he could have their trailer. That is how he views human life, and we make sure that he lives and we as taxpayers give him the best to eat. The prisoners are receiving the best of food, particularly those like Olson, Shearing, Brown and Peters, who are put into special protective areas. They eat a lot better than people on relief and a lot better than people who are unemployed, I will tell you that, Mr. Speaker. If you do not believe me, go to the prisons and see what they are eating. In the Calgary remand centre a short time ago prisoners went on strike because they are getting too much turkey. Well, I know people in my riding who are lucky if they get turkey once a year. That is why the Canadian people are angry.
People say the death penalty is not a deterrent. I happen to believe it is a deterrent. I respect those who think it is not, but I cannot follow their logic. People love life and people will do anything to stay alive. It is only the exceptional person who wants to die. We struggle to remain alive. Some people say that capital punishment is not an effective deterrent, that it is never used. We are told that it did not produce results. Well, it has been a long time since we have had capital punishment, and people knew they would be hanged or executed if they committed a murder. It was in 1961 or 1962 that the last person was hanged in Canada. After that, every murderer was pardoned by a royal pardon. It became a policy of the Government, both Liberal and Conservative, to pardon the person who took another's life. It is too bad they could not bring back the lives which were taken.
How do people know that the death penalty is not a deterrent? From 1961 to 1967 murders kept increasing. In 1963, murders went up 1.04 per 100,000 per year on an average. In 1966, they went up to 1.2. In 1969, they went up to 1.67. In 1972, they went up to 2.05. In 1975, they went up to 2.46, and that was the peak. That was also the time when the death penalty was abolished altogether. Many people tell us to look at the years from 1978 to 1981 when the number of murders dropped from 2.46 to 2.38. But I do not believe that proves anything. I do not really believe statistics prove a great deal either. How many of us know how many murderers would be deterred if they knew they were going to be executed? They love life.
It does not matter what kind of law you have, some murders will be committed, murders of passion which happen in a moment over a family fight, a love affair, or many other instances. It just simply happens. It is not planned and deliberate. Those are a different type of murder. I speak now of those murders which are deliberately planned and executed by these people who know they are not going to be executed but are

May 7, 1984
Capital Punishment
going to be given number one treatment in our jails, and that is what we are giving them.
In my view, the death penalty is a deterrent. It is an effective tool which pinpoints law and order. I respect the views of people who do not believe in capital punishment, even though I cannot follow their logic in light of things which are happening today. The abolitionists appear to have no objection to punishing a child for stealing or a grownup for committing rape. There is no objection to punishing them. But when someone is murdered, the worst of all crimes, then the appropriate punishment is objected to, namely, death to the killer. Violent crimes are becoming all too rampant throughout Canada. Elderly men and women are afraid to walk outside after dark in some of our cities. But we are more concerned about the criminal, in rehabilitating him, than we are about the victims of the crime. The rights of law-abiding citizens seem to be eroding with the increasing leniency toward crime in prison sentences and punishment.
When we get these people in prison, what rights do we take away from them? The only punishment is that they are locked behind bars. That is all. They have better food than many people outside of prison who are honest and clean living. They have entertainment. They are even provided with movies, which many of us would not go to see, blue movies. They have the best of pool tables. Oh, yes, we treat them wonderfully well. We are rehabilitating them. We give them sexual therapy, and what happens? We are now providing conjugal visits at the expense of the taxpayers for prisoners serving a life sentence. We do not even stop with those who are married; we even give this privilege to those who are not married. That is the way we are operating our prisons. Common law wives can go in for conjugal visits at the expense of the taxpayer. Sometimes I wonder why we do not take the prostitutes away from our main hotels and put up a sign in front of our prisons saying, "March up and down here. Government will provide a trailer for you". I hope that is not the next program because it is almost that bad now.
Yes, we must provide food, clothes and shelter, but let us forget about all this bleeding heart business on the pretense of rehabilitating these people. If they did not know what they were doing, that is one thing, but when they know what they are doing, death is the proper punishment. I make no excuse or alibi for advocating that very thing.
I believe that the death penalty is a just punishment when someone deliberately plans to take the life of another human being and carries that plan out, particularly when the victims are young children and women. That is the kind of man Olson was, a yellow dog. He could not pick on a man his own size; he picked on kids or on women. The death penalty, in my view, is a deterrent. We have not given it a chance. We have not had the sure penalty of death on the books long enough for people who deliberately plan and kill and are found guilty beyond the shadow of a doubt. It has not been on the books long enough to show whether or not it is a deterrent, and I believe it is.
The death penalty prevents a second, third and fourth murder, as in the case of Boden. The school teacher in Calgary
would still be teaching youngsters, helping people, if she had not been strangled by this man they call "Strangler Bill". The death sentence is a basic of justice in law. The death penalty is final because there can be no change after a murderer is executed. The courts must be sure that a person is executed only if and when that person is proved guilty beyond the shadow of a doubt to have murdered a child, a woman, a man, a guard, a policeman, another human being. If there is any doubt, then the murderer should be put in prison and not executed. What are we going to do with all these murderers as our prisons get fuller and fuller? Some day we will have so many murderers in our prisons that we will have to start building more prisons, another expense for the taxpayer.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that people who kill should get their desserts: execution. Let it be known across the land that that is what it is. I believe that then the number of deaths will decrease because all human beings love life.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Hudecki (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on the issue of capital punishment. The Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has introduced a Bill to reinstate the death penalty for first degree murder, and I wholeheartedly disagree with that suggestion. I am disappointed that a man of his stature should have killing as the thrust of his speech. The psychology of killing appears to pervade an increasing proportion of our society. We see it in the killing of the unborn and those who are born with abnormalities. We see the thought pervading hospitals when they bring in a person with a broken hip who appears to have difficulty in orientation and in understanding what is going on. The thrust of this psychology of killing is really that we are seeking vengeance, and the more vengeance we seek, the more we promote the concept of killing.
In our system of justice, which is of very high calibre, there have been two cases of people found guilty of murder, and later their innocence was proven. Fortunately, they had been put in prison and not executed. It would have been a sad reflection on our system of justice had we lost those two men.
In 1976, Parliament had a free vote on capital punishment. The result was approval of the Bill officially bringing capital punishment to an end. Instead, as the Hon. Member for Bow River indicated, we have a imposed sentence of life imprisonment with no parole for at least 25 years for first-degree murder and 10 to 15 years for second-degree murder. However, it appears that that vote did not settle the matter. Since then there has been a stream of Private Members' Bills, motions and proposals for a national referendum on the subject. What has this accomplished? Absolutely nothing. Just a lot of window dressing about procedures governing appeals and executions.
There is only one point to be debated here, that is whether or not we want to bring back capital punishment. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we have to ask ourselves why this particular subject keeps coming back. We have to look at it in perspec-
May 7, 1984

tive. We have heard, and probably will hear, numerous arguments about the effectiveness of capital punishment as a deterrent. Statistics can be marshalled to show that the murder rate has not increased since capital punishment has been abolished. Reference will be made to trends in other western abolished. Reference will be made to trends in other western countries. However, I would like to deal with the moral question, because I think that is the key to understanding why this issue keeps coming up. It is perhaps also the key to determining whether or not the matter should once again be put to a vote in the House.
First, Mr. Speaker, every time those who favour capital punishment raise the matter, they inevitably give lurid and emotional examples of murders which have occurred recently. We hear examples of cold-blooded murders in individual ridings. Members do surveys of their constituents and find that a significant percentage are in favour of capital punishment. What these samples illustrate is but one side of the moral issue, namely, that everyone is outraged and horrified by such extreme crimes. No one wants to see a criminal get away with his crime. Every time a murder is committed we hear demands that the death penalty be brought back. Thus it is clear that for the anti-abolitionist the central issue is a moral one.
However, this is stating only one side of a difficult moral question. Those who keep introducing motions to reinstate capital punishment tend to ignore the other half of the problem, that is, whether the state has the right to take a human life deliberately. The right to life is given explicit recognition in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It is not sufficient for anti-abolitionists to argue an eye for an eye. In other areas the state does not punish a crime in the same way it was committed. For example, we do not mutilate those who have been convicted of the crime of mutilation. I seriously question whether the appropriate punishment for the crime of murder is a corresponding act of murder by the state, and I have yet to hear any persuasive arguments to this effect from the other side.
I note the statements by those in favour of hanging that crime is on the upswing and we have lost our morality, that we must do something about these crimes. Well, if indeed Parliament, the criminal justice system or this Government did nothing about crime, then obviously it would be acting immorally. The fact is-and I think we can take some comfort from this solid fact-that Canadians enjoy an effective, sophisticated criminal justice system. The great majority of criminals, including killers, are apprehended by the police. The penalties provided in the Criminal Code for serious offences are severe, and I have noticed no reluctance on the part of the courts to impose such sentences. In 1977, capital punishment was replaced with a mandatory life sentence without eligibility for parole for 25 years. We certainly are not coddling criminals or acting immorally in handing out such sentences, but I hasten to point out that unfortunately in Question Period today details were presented to us by the Solicitor General (Mr. Kaplan) indicating that in a particular situation the implementation of such sentences is wanting. However, he has assured
Capital Punishment
the House that this is an exception and will be fully investigated and appropriate measures taken.
Those who are in favour of capital punishment have the burden of proving that this form of execution by the state is justified. It seems to me that this ultimate penalty carries with it the seeds of severe injustice through its potentially unequal application to the poor. It is very rare that we see the rich, well supported and knowledgeable people go on to an execution. Usually they are able to get the support of the best criminal lawyers in the country. Through the use of their status in life, the support of their friends and the very skilful use of the laws, they are able to have their crime dealt with by a sentence other than execution. If you study the records, you will see that it is usually the ignorant and uneducated who are found guilty and who in so many cases have been, and in some countries still are, executed. So there is a very definite potential for error. This was demonstrated lately in the cases which have been mentioned. This has happened despite elaborate safeguards and guarantees built into our criminal justice system.
The definition problem also makes it difficult for the state to impose the death penalty fairly. However shocking some of the particular examples described, it is likely that many of these crimes would not constitute first degree murder given the emotional element of the crime and the lack of premeditation. These aspects of a crime are very difficult to prove and errors can occur. Moreover, I have heard it argued by retentionists that those who kill are sick, incurable souls. We do not execute the sick. We try to control them, through incarceration if necessary, in order to prevent repetition of their crimes.
It is often suggested that the majority of Canadians want capital punishment, the conclusion from this being that the Government must respect their wishes. The results of the Gallup poll which the Hon. Member has given us are certainly most impressive. However, he was not able to give us the circumstance under which those polls were taken. What were the factors that stimulated such a response at that time and place?
I believe that we must confront the moral issue, particularly in terms of our roles as MPs. Certainly the majority of Canadians do not want to pay taxes, for example, but no one is suggesting that we stop taxing. Our democratic system does not require that each MP vote every time according to the wishes of the majority of his constituents. That is not our role as Members of Parliament. This is particularly true of moral and philosophical issues like this one. His or her decisions must be based on reason, evidence and a sense of the morality of the issue. I believe that this principle of parliamentary democracy was articulated centuries ago by Edmund Burke, and I am willing to be guided by that well-known conservative.
There also appears to be a trend in the United States in favour of executing people by pills or lethal injections, as though this made execution somehow more humane, as if it was simply a matter of putting someone out of their misery.

May 7, 1984
Capital Punishment
The first such execution was carried out in Texas in December of 1982 on a prisoner named Charlie Brooks. In effect, they gave him a massive drug overdose to kill him. Whether we kill someone by hanging, shooting or by passing 2,000 volts of electricity through his body, we cannot sidestep the fundamental moral issue of whether or not this meditated killing by the state is justified.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I have chosen to emphasize the moral question in this capital punishment controversy. The 1976 free vote was a culmination of years of public debate on the issue. Approximately half the Members of the House at that time spoke on this matter. I know that many of them agonized over the moral question. Ultimately, Members voted according to their conscience, and the result was a majority in favour of abolition. The issue has not changed since this wide-ranging debate in 1976. I cannot see what would be gained by returning to the issue in a free vote.
Yes, there will continue to be horrifying examples of murder. I stress that these incidents will probably occur regardless of whether or not we have capital punishment. Members can conduct public opinion polls of their constituents, but it is not our role collectively to vote strictly according to public opinion surveys. The issue keeps coming up because it is a moral issue. It seems to me that in the 1976 debate the moral questions, from both sides, received a full and fair hearing.
I do not have the time to deal at length with the huge subject of deterrence, which is a moral question in itself. I would like to quote from an essay by Albert Camus, the Nobel Prize winner and passionate opponent of capital punishment. He said:
It cannot be denied, however, that men fear death. The privation of life is indeed the supreme penalty and ought to excite in them a decisive fear. The fear of death, arising from the most obscure depths of the individual, ravished him; the instinct to live, when it is threatened, panics and struggles in agony. Therefore the legislator was right in thinking that his law was based upon one of the most mysterious and most powerful incentives of human nature. But law is always simpler than nature. When law ventures, in the hope of dominating, into the dark regions of consciousness, it has little chance of being able to simplify the complexity it wants to codify.
If fear of death is, indeed, a fact, another fact is that such fear, however great it may be, has never sufficed to quell human passions.
The proof of this argument is that capital punishment has never succeeded in eliminating murder. I suggest that our strong and fair system of justice, including the criminal law, has shown itself to be a better approach to deterring criminal acts. It imposes appropriate punishments but, perhaps more important, it fosters respect for the law. The Government has also implemented firm gun control measures and is embarking upon crime prevention efforts that I believe will result in significantly reducing the opportunity to commit crimes.
I have heard no compelling reasons for reopening debate on an issue which has received as much House time over the last 30 years as any other single matter.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak on Bill C-214, an Act to amend the Criminal Code. I feel very strongly that we need
a review before the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in order to review some of the more recent statistics we have as a result of the abolition of capital punishment.
I would like to take a moment, Mr. Speaker, to discuss a couple of points that were brought up by the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki). First, there seems to be an inclination among members of both the Liberal and the New Democratic Party to refer in the House to cases in which people would have been hanged. They talk about two cases in which a person who was found guilty would not be alive today if the death penalty were in force. These people have since been found innocent. I remind both of these Parties that in both occasions, and in particular in the Don Marshall case in Nova Scotia, the charge was not first degree murder but second degree murder. The courts did not find the murder to be premeditated in the case of Donald Marshall. That person would not have been hanged had the law implementing capital punishment for premeditated first degree murder been in place.
The other point that was made by the Member for Hamilton West was that there was one strong point to be made, to paraphrase his comment, which is, that murders have not increased since the abolition of the death penalty. I would like to take this opportunity to point out to the Hon. Member that according to the statistics of Statistics Canada, it is the number of first degree murders committed while in the act of committing a criminal offence that have increased. That means murders while robbing a Beckers, a Mac's Milk or actions of that nature. The deterrent to carry a gun is not there, particularly a loaded gun.
Therefore, it is grossly unfair to say that, because we do not have capital punishment and because there is a decrease in first degree murders, we do not need capital punishment. If we could decrease the number of first degree murders that have occurred while in the act of committing a criminal offence by the deterrent of carrying a loaded gun, that would go a long way. I remind the Hon. Member that the number of first degree murders was decreasing when capital punishment was in place according to a great number of Statistics Canada figures. First degree murders were on a decline and they are still on a decline, thanks to the improvement in society. It still does not answer the question of when constituents feel that there needs to be a review of this very important question.
With respect to deterrents, there are those like myself who feel that it would definitely be a deterrent and there are those who feel differently. With all due respect, there are people who are probably far more expert in analysing the pros and cons of capital punishment than are most Members of Parliament, including myself. We cannot afford the disadvantage of not reviewing such an issue from time to time. Simply because we abolished capital punishment in 1976 does not mean that it should be abolished forever. There have been many types of legislation that have been put in place and either have not been
May 7, 1984

implemented by the Government or have been overlooked or else have been amended as time have changed.
As far as violence while in the act of committing a criminal offence is concerned, I am sure the Hon. Member who is in support of abolition was horrified by the Barbara Turnbull case. She is an 18-year old girl from Mississauga, who was a Beckers' store clerk and also a volunteer worker with terminally ill cancer patients, who was shot in September, 1983, and now is paralyzed for life. I am sure he is also aware of the Nizam Ali case. He was an 18-year old boy who was stabbed to death recently while he worked the overnight shift at a fast food dispensing store. Constable David Utman is another example. He was a 38-year old Nepean police force officer who was shot to death at a west end shopping centre on October 14, 1983. The accused, one Peter M. Collins, escaped in June from the regional detention centre where he was awaiting trial on several robbery charges. I am convinced that bringing in capital punishment for premeditated first degree murder would deter us from carrying a loaded gun.
I am not picking on the Member for Hamilton West but he is the only member on the government side who has spoken on this issue so far. I would like to make one other point in response to his comments. During his remarks in reference to the remarks of the Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) who introduced Bill C-214 he said that he "could not substantiate the poll". I challenge the Member for Hamilton West to take his own poll. Let the Member ask a very simple question of the constituents in his riding. Let him ask if they support capital punishment for premeditated first degree murder, yes or no. I challenge him or any other Members of the House to take the same poll.
Surely, when Gallup takes a poll, it is a national poll. They do not look for the riding that has just experienced a most horrendous murder. They do it on a regular basis, and there has never been a poll taken in Canada that has demonstrated the support of abolition by a majority of people.
I believe that we as Members of Parliament have a certain obligation to our constituents who send us to Ottawa to represent them. It is not satisfactory simply to say that we abolished the death penalty in 1976 by a majority of six votes and so we have abolished it forever.
I remind Hon. Members that when we abolished the death penalty for first degree murder in 1976, I am sure that a great number of those in the House today who were here then have perhaps changed their minds. I know that I used to be an abolitionist. I am the son of a United Church Minister who fought long and hard for many years to see the death penalty abolished. When I came to Ottawa in 1979, I was still an abolitionist.
However, there comes a point in the conscience of every Member of Parliament when he or she must determine on many of these issues whether he or she will vote one of three ways; either for the position taken by the Party, on what he or she believes to be the majority wishes of the constituents, or on his or her own conscience. I found it very difficult as a Member of Parliament to satisfy my conscience when I voted
Capital Punishment
against 87 per cent of the constituents in my riding. I did not ask that question if the people in my riding at a time when there was a horrendous murder case described on the front pages of any daily newspaper in Canada. In fact, I pointed out to them that I thought that the people in my riding might have changed and that there was a feeling that there might be a desire to maintain the abolitionist viewpoint. I was prepared to listen to my constituents, 87 per cent of whom voted to return to the death penalty for premeditated first degree murder.
I would be remiss if I did not take this opportunity to answer some of the questions that are so often asked of Members of Parliament who support capital punishment for premeditated first degree murder.
In addition to what has already been stated, the following points illustrate why it is favourable, in my humble estimation, to have capital punishment for premeditated murder reinstated. First, public opinion appears to be in favour of the death penalty. In a democracy, the will of the majority should be respected.
Second, the alternative of life imprisonment or 25 years of mandatory imprisonment may be harsher and more cruel punishment than death. Some prisoners in the position of facing this kind of alternative have voiced this kind of opinion publicly.
Third, in response to the argument that the state does not have the right to take a person's life, think what the state can do in wartime. One will see that the state has established the right to take another man's life.
Fourth, the victim's family should be a major factor in fitting the punishment to the crime. Next, the rate in Canada of homicidal offences generally and murder incidents in particular has more than doubled from 1961 to 1978. At a time when violent crime is increasing, the focus should be on the maximum possible protection of society rather than on the treatment of the criminal.
The final point is that in 1956, the parliamentary joint committee, after serious study, recommended retention of the death penalty.
I would say that the principle of democratic representation is a greater one than that of any single cause, whether or not, for the best of reasons, Members are convinced of their own rightness of action which is contrary to the clear opinion of the majority of their constituents. I for one do not quibble with, or seek to argue, the rights or wrongs of the case, although I have my own opinion about that. What I seek to defend is the right of the people to exert their will. This right, I feel, should supersede the right of government within the limits of order to exert its will if that is contrary to the peoples' will.
Finally, the principle of a free vote is far preferable to the muzzle which has been imposed on certain sections of seats in this House when it suits the purposes of certain interests. I say that with good reason. We had an Opposition Day motion to be considered publicly not as a vote of confidence or non-confi-

May 7, 1984
Capital Punishment
dence in the Government two years ago in the House. It was introduced by the Conservative Opposition. We asked for no more, no less than that the subject of capital punishment be referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and legal Affairs in order that we could review up-dated information, perhaps so that we could convince the abolitionists that we should have capital punishment or perhaps so that we could convince those in support of capital punishment that we should retain abolition. That is the democratic process. All government Members plus five Members in Opposition voted against even talking about it. That says something about Government and its lack of credibility in representing constituents when 80-some per cent of constituents in most polls and 70-some per cent of constituents in national Gallup polls support capital punishment for premeditated first degree murder.
What I would like to see happen with this Bill brought in by the Hon. Member for Bow River is to see it referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs in order that expert witnesses from the John Howard Society and organizations that speak very strongly in support of abolition could be called so that all Members of Parliament would have a better understanding of the pros and cons of capital punishment. Failing that, Mr. Speaker, in order to carry the case before the House of Commons, we have to resort to Opposition Days, asking questions in the House, making statements under Standing Order 21, through Private Members Bills and through statements on motions as well as every other means we can conjure up so that someone can give some fair representation to constituents who send Members here to Ottawa to represent them.
It is seven minutes to six o'clock. I do not want to be accused of talking out this Bill. I am sure that if I sit down now there will probably be no other speakers and we could refer the subject matter of the Member for Bow River's Bill to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first time in my years in Parliament that I have spoken on this question. I have voted on this question three times. I voted for abolition on each occasion. The people of my constituency who are part of that large majority which the polls tell us favour capital punishment knew my position and had the opportunity to end my career as a Member of Parliament if they thought that this was an issue that was so important and an issue on which I was so at odds with them that I ought not to continue to be a Member. But I am still here, Mr. Speaker.
I want to remind those Members who have spoken in support of capital punishment, and I respect their right to hold their views, that we have had three votes on this question. The last time we had this vote, the vote for abolition was supported by the Leaders of all three Parties, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the present Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), and the Rt. Hon. Member for Bow River, who was then the Leader of the Conservative Party.
Mr. Speaker, I rise-

I am sorry, Mr. Speaker. I meant the Right Hon. former Prime Minister. He is not the Member from Bow River. Let me remind Members of Parliament that the Gallup polls in Great Britain show a similar support for capital punishment. I remind Members of Parliament here that the British Parliament recently had a free vote.
Good.

The British Parliament has a majority of members who are Conservative. The Government is led by the Prime Minister who is a supporter of capital punishment. The British Parliament again voted on the question and again rejected bringing back capital punishment.
What is wrong with that?
In virtually every democratic country, Mr. Speaker-
Except Canada.

-Norway, Sweden, Holland, Denmark, Belgium, France, Spain, Australia, New Zealand, and Israel, all of them have abolished capital punishment. The State of Israel has the kind of problem that we will never have. It has terrorists operating almost daily. When Israel wanted to execute Adolf Eichmann for the millions of deaths for which he was responsible, Israel had to pass a special Act which applied only to Adolf Eichmann.
You will never get that chance in Canada.
Those countries have abolished capital punishment. The countries which have not abolished capital punishment are the military dictatorships of South America, communist countries-
The United States.

-such as the Soviet Union, China. Those are the countries which have capital punishment. I see no reason that I should follow the example of those countries on the question of capital punishment or on any other question. I see every reason for following the example which we have seen in virtually all democratic countries which have abolished capital punishment and which, incidentally, have among the lowest rates and numbers of murder of any countries in the world.
We have figures for the number and rates of murders which have occurred since the abolition of capital punishment. The facts are pretty clear, Mr. Speaker. The numbers and rate have decreased. In 1975, we had 701 murders. This figure includes manslaughter and infanticide. In 1980, the last year for which I have figures, that number is down to 593. The rate was 3.07. That figure is now down to 2.48. The rate is determined on the basis of offences per 100,000 of the population.
All the evidence is that capital punishment does not work as a deterrent. If it does not work as a deterrent, the only argument for capital punishment disappears. That being the
May 7, 1984

case, I would vote again, as I have on earlier occasions, for abolition.

Mr. Speaker, thank you for giving me the floor. I suppose I could speak to this subject for at least half an hour, but since we only have one minute left until six o'clock, I have no objection if the House agrees to call it six o'clock, I think it is not really worthwhile to start a speech with one minute left. Could the House give me its opinion?
In order to do that, we need unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent to call it six o'clock?
Agreed.
No.

Mr. Speaker, we do not have the unanimous consent of the House to interrupt the debate, and we only have about thirty seconds left. I wonder whether I should start my speech. Actually, the abolition of capital punishment was adopted by the House on July 14, 1976, for a variety of good reasons and after lengthy debate.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the Bill presented in the House by the Hon. Member-

subtopic: CANADIAN DEVELOPMENT INVESTMENT CORPORATION-STATUS OF ORDERS FOR DASH-8 AIRCRAFT MANUFACTURED BY DE HAVILLAND. (B) FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE OFFERED TO AIRLINE COMPANIES
CANADIAN DEVELOPMENT INVESTMENT CORPORATION-STATUS OF ORDERS FOR DASH-8 AIRCRAFT MANUFACTURED BY DE HAVILLAND. (B) FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE OFFERED TO AIRLINE COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to enter into the record information concerning the Dash-8 aircraft and the sale of this aircraft by de Havilland to three domestic Canadian airline companies. In
Adjournment Debate
telephone conversations today, I was advised that there is very little now standing in the way of the Government of Canada co-operating through the Crown corporation, de Havilland, so that these $60 million to $100 million worth of Dash-8s are sold to the three Canadian airline companies.
What good is an aircraft company in Canada if we cannot sell the aircraft to our domestic airlines? Atonabee Airways, a Peterborough company, has now moved its headquarters to Toronto. What is standing in the way of the sale of millions of dollars of aircraft by de Havilland to Air Atonabee, Time Air of Lethbridge and Norcanair of Saskatoon? It is very simple.
Competition in Ireland has come in with a comparable aircraft. It developed in its private sector an aircraft that seats 36, the same number of people, flies at less cost per mile and costs $2 million per aircraft less. It will sell to the Canadian passenger aircraft industry for over $2 million less per unit. In addition, it will sell with an interest rate of 7 per cent to Air Atonabee in Toronto.
What does the Government have to do in order to save the industry? I would point out that a loss of $100 million worth of business to de Havilland represents an immediate lay-off of 400 employees. It means cutting the work force from 2,450 to under 2,000 and a forecast of future lay-offs. The Canadian Government has dumped $700 million into de Havilland to build an airplane that cannot be marketed because of poor management on the part of a Crown corporation. That Crown corporation is directly accountable to the Cabinet. Regardless of whether or not the Economic Development Minister says we should get rid of it, the point is that we have put a lot of money into de Havilland and Canadair. Those who go on the air to talk about getting rid of these two companies have little compassion for the 2,450 employees at de Havilland.
We are not interfering, as the Minister would have us believe, with our GATT agreements when we offer to subsidize interest rates in order to compete on the international market in a domestic situation. We in the Opposition are asking the Government to take a very close look at the situation that now prevails. An Irish firm is offering 7 per cent interest to Atonabee Airways on the purchase of planes for $2 million less. We have invested $700 million in de Havilland and the Government is not prepared to subsidize the interest rates. Where is the justice that is required on behalf of those employees?
If that is not bad enough, Jack Austin appeared on Canada AM just last week and stated that we should be subsidizing interest rates to the tune of 2 per cent. I do not know what he meant by that. There is no one with any sense to answer for him in the House of Commons. All the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) has said is that we are not in the business of subsidizing these industries in order for them to sell aircraft. If we are not in that business, then why did we dump $700 million into a company so it could build an aircraft that we cannot market?

May 7, 1984
Adjournment Debate
I plead with the Government of Canada and with the Minister's Parliamentary Secretary who will respond to me to answer the question. Are we going to susidize Air Atonabee and de Havilland aircraft so that we can sell the Dash-8s or are we going to let $100 million go out the window through Time Air, Norcanair and Air Atonabee, and satisfy ourselves by saying that we have some strange agreement with GATT? This is a domestic matter. Another country has entered Canada and has undercut our own Crown corporation. I plead with the Government to meet the interest rate. If it can do it to build monuments in Algeria, it should be able to do it to sell aicraft.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: CANADIAN DEVELOPMENT INVESTMENT CORPORATION-STATUS OF ORDERS FOR DASH-8 AIRCRAFT MANUFACTURED BY DE HAVILLAND. (B) FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE OFFERED TO AIRLINE COMPANIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) is to be congratulated for keeping this matter before the House. He does make a good point. When he has asked what good the aircraft industry in Canada is if we cannot sell to airlines in Canada, he makes a very valid point indeed, and one which we must take a very good look at. Unfortunately, the time that is available to me will not allow me to respond to all of the matters raised by the Hon. Member. It is too bad that we could not have a full-scale debate on this issue because I think it is one that is worthy of that kind of consideration.
When this issue first arose a few weeks ago, a great many false impressions were created regarding the status of potential purchases of the Dash-8 by Air Atonabee of Peterborough, Ontario, Time Air of Alberta and Norcanair of Saskatoon. Let me correct the record.
First, Air Atonabee had then and has now five conditional contracts for the Dash-8. There have been no cancellations of contracts. Second, Time Air had a contract for four Dash-8s. The contract was conditional on the availability of satisfactory sales financing. Time Air gave notice of cancellation because of a lack of this financing. The two parties are now discussing a new contract. Third, Norcanair has not signed a contract but is currently negotiating a contract for three Dash-8s. In the last two weeks, representatives of all three airlines have witnessed demonstration flights of the Dash-8. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, they really like that plane.
I hope that this will clear the air on the current status of de Havilland's dealings with those companies. All of these airlines would prefer to buy the Dash-8. That is why they are pressing so hard for financing concessions. They are tightly run enterprises with limited margins and must be extremely conscious of costs. This means that competitors offering low-interest sales financing have great appeal for Canadian regional operators. What Members have seen is a public lobbying effort to get a government decision on the type of competitive sales financing de Havilland may be able to offer. The pressure reflects the fact that these operators would sooner buy the Dash-8.
Embraer Brasilia is an example of what we are up against. Brazil has offered 10-year 90 per cent financing at interest rates as low as 7.5 per cent in Canada. This may be compared
with the roughly 13.5 per cent interest rates which domestic carriers can negotiate with Canadian financial institutions.
The 360 Short aircraft has been named publicly as one that is taking customers from de Havilland. I must tell the House that this aircraft is not comparable to the Dash-8. It is unpressurized, which means it cannot fly above 10,000 feet and therefore cannot climb to avoid turbulence. It is also slower than the Dash-8. It is unlikely that the flying public would want to use this plane for any but the shortest flights.
