subtopic: PROVINCIAL AFFAIRS-CHURCHILL FALLS POWER CONTRACT- GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: PROVINCIAL AFFAIRS-CHURCHILL FALLS POWER CONTRACT- GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last, that is May 3, the Supreme Court of Canada brought down a unanimous decision respecting the Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act. They declared that legislation to be ultra vires, that is to say unconstitutional. That was a Bill which was brought in and passed by the Newfoundland legislature in 1980 to give the Government of Newfoundland the authority to withhold the water that was the source of power for the Churchill Falls Corporation Limited. The legislation was referred to the Supreme Court of Newfoundland by the Government of Newfoundland, in order to be sure it was on clear constitutional grounds. It was ruled by that court, in fact, to be constitutional. The Government of Newfoundland then referred it on to the highest court in the land, the Supreme Court of Canada.
I might have raised the question that day, to the Government of Canada, as to what steps it proposed to take with regard to the impact and the consequences of the decision. I did not because I wanted to wait 24 hours so as not to be seen to be emotionally shooting from the hip or, more precisely, to have an opportunity to examine the judgment and the consequences flowing from it. I raised the question on the following day, May 4. It can be found at page 3412 of Hansard. I put the question to the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Pepin). I served notice that I would be raising the question, because I knew that the Prime Minsiter (Mr. Trudeau) would not be in the House that day and I wanted the acting Prime Minister to be fully briefed. I put the question to the Acting Prime Minister as to what steps the Government of Canada intended to take to see that justice was done in this case. The Supreme Court of Canada addressed itself to the strict points of the law-to the letter of the law. They said that someone else would have to deal with the social and political ramifications of the legislation.
The genesis of Newfoundland's Upper Churchill Water Rights Reversion Act goes back to 1969, when the Government of Newfoundland through its agency, the Churchill Falls Corporation, entered into a long-term agreement with Quebec Hydro. It was a 65-year agreement for the sale of power from the Churchill Falls development to Hydro Quebec. The Quebec Government of the day made it very clear to the
May 7, 1984

Newfoundland Government that if they did not sell the power to Quebec they would not be able to sell the power to anybody. In other words, Newfoundland would not be able to transmit its power through the Province of Quebec. Therefore, Newfoundland was forced to enter into a 65-year contract to sell that power for 2.5 mills.
That power is being sold today to New York State and to some of the New England states, as well as to the Province of New Brunswick and, to a lesser extent, the Province of Ontario, for 28 mills. The Economic Council of Canada estimated the income to the Province of Quebec to be $800 million. The income derived from that power to the people of Newfoundland-the owner of the resource-has been estimated to be $8 million. It is clearly a situation that cannot be condoned and cannot be allowed to continue.
The Acting Prime Minister, in reply to my question, said that it was a provincial matter. Clearly it is not a provincial matter because it deals with interprovincial trade, it deals with international trade, it deals with the National Energy Board and it deals with the National Energy Program. Under the Constitution all of these are clearly within federal jurisdiction. While the Acting Prime Minister was saying that it was a provincial matter, his colleague, the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Rompkey), was saying outside of this House that he felt the federal Government should have been involved in this matter.
How can the federal Government get involved? There are a number of ways. First of all, it must recognize that this injustice cannot be condoned and cannot continue. Second, it must recognize that we cannot hope to achieve justice from a government in Quebec that is dedicated to the separation and the breaking up of this country. We cannot expect to get just treatment from a separatist government in Quebec. Third, the Government must recognize that this power belongs to the people of Newfoundland, and should enjoy the same rights of passage as natural gas coming from the western provinces. When the Government of Canada builds a pipeline, it does not have to ask the Province of Manitoba or the Province of Ontario for permission to build the pipelines in order to get the gas into the markets of Montreal. We demand nothing less in terms of hydro power.
The purport of my question on Friday was to ask the Government of Canada in the name of justice, in the name of simple justice, if it would invoke the powers it has under the National Energy Program, specifically under the National Energy Board, to treat the transmission of hydro electric power in the same way as we treat the transmission of other sources of energy, for example, gas, in terms of declaring it in the national interest that common carriers carry this power across the Province of Quebec and into the markets of Ontario and New England so that Newfoundland could enjoy the revenue.
We are a poor province, Sir. We have had a number of blows. We pay the second highest domestic electric rates in the
Adjournment Debate
country in St. John's, Newfoundland. I believe Charlottetown pays the highest. The City of Montreal, I believe, pays the lowest domestic electricity rates. That is because of the power it enjoys from a Newfoundland resource.
I said to the Prime Minister that this was a festering sore on the face of Canada and unless something was done to correct it, unless there was remedial action, there would be dire consequences. The people of Newfoundland have been much harder hit by this decision than by the decision with respect to the offshore oil and gas. Clearly this is perceived by every man, woman and child who has the power of judgment and rationality to be a gross injustice to the people of Newfoundland. I can only say to you, Sir, that if corrective steps are not taken it will fan the fires of separatism of which I hope the Government will take notice.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PROVINCIAL AFFAIRS-CHURCHILL FALLS POWER CONTRACT- GOVERNMENT POSITION. (B) NATIONAL ENERGY BOARD ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in order to add to the remarks made on May 4 by the Minister of External Relations (Mr. Pepin), I would make the following comments: trade in oil and gas and in other commodities which involve the bulk transfer of a natural resource between a source province and a number of receiving provinces lends itself readily to the concept of a common carrier for transportation. Electricity trade, on the other hand, has generally involved interchanges between complex electric power systems that include generation facilities and customer loads. These systems usually involve multiple transmission linkages, making it technically difficult to identify definite paths for a specific flow of power and energy. For this reason, interchanges within power pools and between individual utilities have quite generally in North America been handled through a series of contractual agreements for "wheeling", by which is meant the transfer of electricity over transmission systems.
The power conferred upon the National Energy Board, under its Act, provides for the authorization of construction of designated interprovincial and international transmission lines. This would provide, for example, the assurance that interconnections could be built even if provincial statutes did not provide powers for the province to authorize such facilities for extra-provincial purposes. These powers do not envisage common carrier facilities. No application has yet been received for interprovincial lines and there is no proposal to make any changes to legislation at the present time.

subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-SIZE OF ANNOUNCED PAY-OUT. (B) CONTRIBUTIONS TO FUND
WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-SIZE OF ANNOUNCED PAY-OUT. (B) CONTRIBUTIONS TO FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 3, I directed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) which is recorded at page 3681 of Hansard as follows:
-my question is supplemental to those asked of the Minister of Agriculture with regard to the Grain Stabilization Fund. When is this pay-out going to be made?
The Minister of Agriculture replied:
-I am sure the Hon. Member knows that the legislation has to be changed, et cetera. The formula has to be approved by the House through the necessary

May 7, 1984
Adjournment Debate
procedures. Unless we have the speedy concurrence of the House, we would be very lucky to make one in 1984. However, we want to do it in 1984.
Then as recorded at page 2711 of Hansard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) this question:
The Prime Minister is aware of the growing concern of western grain farmers because of the Government's delay in carrying out its commitment to amend the Grain Stabilization Act to permit desperately needed cash payments this spring. Will the Prime Minister prod his lethargic Ministers to bring down the legislation so that hard-pressed grain farmers in western Canada can have the assurance right now of desperately needed cash flow at this time?
The Prime Minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I would be in a better position to give that assurance to the Hon. Leader of the Opposition if he were to assure me that his Party would co-operate with the Government House Leader in getting through that and many other pieces of legislation which the country needs.
Then as recorded at page 2713 of Hansard the Leader of the Opposition said:
It is typical of the Government that when the interests of western Canada are involved, it is always tied to something else. You can't get a straight answer from the Government.
The Hon. Otto Lang proposed this legislation to the House of Commons. We told him at that time it would not work, but he was stubborn, would not listen, and now western grain producers are suffering the consequences. On April 4, the Prime Minister said that the legislation passed by the Liberal Government in 1976 had to be corrected. We are still waiting for the amendments.
The western grain producers are not asking for something which is not theirs by right. There is $1 billion in that fund, a third of which was contributed by the producer. That was the agreement, however, inept it was, that the Government of the day made with western grain producers. We had a promise of a pay-out in October, but the farmers need it now. The pay-out is supposed to be in the vicinity of $300 million. That is less than one third of the balance in that account. That means that even with this pay-out the Government is not giving back to the farmers even the amount they put into it. It is unfair, unjust and it is frustrating for the western grain producer.
This year, Mr. Speaker, the western producers will probably contribute about $50 million to this fund. There is now $1 billion in this fund, which means that at 10 per cent interest there will accrue to the fund probably $100 million. That is a total of $ 150 million, subtracted from a $300 million pay-out, leaving a pay-out of only $150 million in fact. The fact that the producer has to wait until the fall to receive this money just creates more distrust and disharmony in the west.
I wanted to bring to your attention and the attention of this House how unjust the Government has been, and is currently in its treatment of the prairie grain producer. There is absolutely no wonder, Mr. Speaker, why the Government cannot
generate any trust or good will in western Canada. If the Government would make they pay-out immediately, then of course the farmer would be getting it at a time he justly deserves it.
Thank you very much for allowing me to bring this to the attention of yourself and this House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT-SIZE OF ANNOUNCED PAY-OUT. (B) CONTRIBUTIONS TO FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Western Grain Stabilization Act was enacted to provide income insurance for those prairie grain producers who wished to be covered. It was designed to be actuarially sound. Normally producers contribute 2 per cent of the value of their grain sales and the Government of Canada contributes an additional 4 per cent. This money is deposited in an interest bearing account, the western grain stabilization fund, for use when prairie grain incomes are depressed.
Because of the actuarial mechanism, contributions were reduced on January 1, 1984 to 1.5 per cent for producers and 3.5 per cent for the Government in light of large fund balances. Proportionately, therefore, producers have benefited more from this, with a 25 per cent reduction, then has the Government, with a 12.5 per cent reduction.
Pay-outs under the original Western Grain Stabilization Act are triggered when net cash flow, which is essentially receipts less cash costs, fall below the previous five year average. Despite lower grain prices over the past two years, total receipts have not fallen because volumes sold have been increasing so that pay-outs have not been triggered.
The intention of the Western Grain Stabilization Act was to have an actuarially sound producer-contributory program. Even in its proposed amended form, it is important to note that the actuarial soundness will be preserved. It would be imprudent to amend the Act in such a way as to undermine its actuarial mechanism, as would be the case if all producer contributions to date were simply reimbursed. This could seriously deplete the fund, leaving inadequate amounts available in case pay-outs are triggered next year or beyond.
The Government intends, however, to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act to make it more responsive to the needs of the prairie grain economy. Under the proposed payout mechanism, participating producers will receive larger and earlier payouts than the existing Act would provide. The actuarial soundness of the program will, however, be maintained so that the funds will continue to be managed in a responsible manner.
